quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 395




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.3 Maximum driving time for property-carrying vehicles.




(a) Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1, no motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, unless the driver complies with the following requirements:




(1) Start of work shift.  A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty;






(2) 14-hour period.  A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.






(3) Driving time and interruptions of driving periods —




(i) Driving time.  A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.






(ii) Interruption of driving time.  Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time.










(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any period of 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or






(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.








(c) 




(1) Any period of 7 consecutive days may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours.





(2) Any period of 8 consecutive days may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours.





[76 FR 81188, Dec. 27, 2011, as amended at 78 FR 58485, Sept. 24, 2013; 78 FR 64181, Oct. 28, 2013; 84 FR 48081, Sept. 12, 2019; 85 FR 33452, June 1, 2020]

verdict.summary:
APPLICABLE RULE AND SCOPE

49 CFR § 395.3(a) governs maximum driving time for property-carrying commercial motor vehicles. Subsection (a) opens with the qualifier 'Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1,' so the three figures below are the baseline rule, subject to the exemptions discussed at the end. The answers below assume the current published text (2025 annual edition / current eCFR), an interstate property-carrying CMV driver requiring a CDL, and no applicable exemption under § 395.1. Passenger-carrying limits (§ 395.5: 10 driving hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, no driving after 15 hours on duty) do not apply.

THE THREE ANSWERS

1) Consecutive off-duty hours required before driving: 10 HOURS.
Source: § 395.3(a)(1) 'Start of work shift. A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty.'
Operation: the 10 hours must be consecutive and must be off duty (off-duty or sleeper-berth status; the regulation states it as off duty). No driving may occur until the full 10 consecutive hours have been completed. This 10-hour period is what resets the 14-hour clock in (a)(2).

2) Consecutive hours after which the driver may no longer drive: 14 HOURS.
Source: § 395.3(a)(2) '14-hour period. A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.'
Operation and precision note: the regulatory quantity is elapsed clock time from the moment the driver comes on duty following the 10-hour break — commonly called the 14-hour driving window — not cumulative 'on duty' time. The distinction matters: any off-duty, sleeper-berth, or on-duty-not-driving time that occurs inside the 14 hours does not pause or extend the window (absent the split-sleeper provision of § 395.1(g) or another § 395.1 exception). Once 14 consecutive hours have elapsed since coming on duty, the driver may not drive, even if the driver has driving hours left under the 11-hour limit. The driver may remain on duty performing non-driving work; the prohibition is on driving.

3) Total hours that may be driven within that period: 11 HOURS.
Source: § 395.3(a)(3)(i) 'Driving time. A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.'
Operation: 11 hours is a cumulative cap on driving time inside the 14-hour window, not a cap on total on-duty time. A driver may be on duty (loading, fueling, paperwork, inspections) beyond 11 hours within the window, but may not drive past the 11th hour of driving or past the 14th hour of elapsed window time, whichever comes first.

SECONDARY REQUIREMENT INSIDE THE SAME PARAGRAPH (for completeness, not one of the three answers)

§ 395.3(a)(3)(ii): except for drivers qualifying for the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), 'driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status.' The 30-minute interruption may be satisfied by off-duty, sleeper berth, on-duty-not-driving time, or any combination. This is a break requirement, not an extension of either the 11-hour or 14-hour limit.

WORKED TIMELINE (illustrating how the three figures interact)

- Day starts: driver has completed 10 consecutive hours off duty. Requirement 1 satisfied.
- 06:00 — driver comes on duty; the 14-hour window starts. It will close at 20:00 regardless of what happens in between.
- 06:00–12:00 — 6 hours driving.
- 12:00–12:30 — 30-minute interruption (on-duty not driving). Break requirement satisfied; window still closes at 20:00.
- 12:30–17:30 — 5 more hours driving. Cumulative driving = 11 hours; the 11-hour cap is now exhausted at 17:30.
- Driver may continue on duty but may not drive after 17:30 (11-hour cap) and in any event may not drive after 20:00 (14-hour window).
- Next driving requires a fresh 10 consecutive hours off duty.

ADJACENT LIMITS NOT ANSWERED HERE (so they are not mistaken for answers to asks 1–3)

- § 395.3(b): no driving after 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day of the week) or 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day). These are cumulative on-duty limits, outside the scope of § 395.3(a) as asked.
- § 395.3(c): a 7- or 8-day period may be ended with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours (the '34-hour restart').

EXCEPTIONS THAT WOULD CHANGE THESE NUMBERS (assumption stated, not applied)

- § 395.1(k)(1) (Alaska, property-carrying): § 395.3(a) and (b) do not apply; the Alaska limits are 15 hours of driving following 10 consecutive hours off duty, no driving after 20 hours on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty, plus 70/80-hour limits. The figure 15 replaces 14 and 20 replaces the 14-hour window in that jurisdiction.
- § 395.1(e) (short-haul): drivers meeting the short-haul conditions are relieved of record-of-duty-status requirements and of the § 395.3(a)(3)(ii) 30-minute break, and operate under the 14-hour/11-hour structure as modified by that section.
- § 395.1(g) (split sleeper berth): allows the 14-hour window and the required 10-hour off-duty period to be recalculated using qualifying sleeper-berth and off-duty periods, which can effectively extend the working window.
- § 395.1(b) (adverse driving conditions) and § 395.1(c) (emergency conditions) permit limited extension of the driving and window limits when their conditions are met.
- Intrastate operations may follow state variants rather than the federal figures.

If any of the above applies to the driver in question, the three values must be re-derived under that provision; the values stated here are the unexcepted § 395.3(a) baseline.

Official interpretation of Paragraph 23(a)(3)
1. Rescission period.
i. The period within which the consumer may exercise the right to rescind runs for 3 business days from the last of 3 events:
A. Consummation of the transaction.
B. Delivery of all material disclosures.
C. Delivery to the consumer of the required rescission notice.
ii. For example:
A. If a transaction is consummated on Friday, June 1, and the disclosures and notice of the right to rescind were given on Thursday, May 31, the rescission period will expire at midnight of the third business day after June 1 - that is, Tuesday, June 5.
B. If the disclosures are given and the transaction consummated on Friday, June 1, and the rescission notice is given on Monday, June 4, the rescission period expires at midnight of the third business day after June 4 - that is, Thursday, June 7. The consumer must place the rescission notice in the mail, file it for telegraphic transmission, or deliver it to the creditor's place of business within that period in order to exercise the right.

verdict.summary:
**Question presented.** Under 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), when may a consumer exercise the right to rescind a covered credit transaction, and when does that right expire if the required notice of rescission or the material disclosures are never delivered?

**Short answer.**
1. **General rule — ask 1.** The consumer may exercise the right until **midnight of the third business day following the last of** (a) consummation, (b) delivery of the notice required by § 1026.23(b), or (c) delivery of all material disclosures. The trigger is the last of those three events, not consummation alone.
2. **Extended rule — ask 2.** If the required notice or material disclosures are never delivered, the right expires at the **earliest of** (a) **3 years after consummation**, (b) **transfer of all of the consumer’s interest in the property**, or (c) **sale of the property**.

**Governing text.** Section 1026.23(a)(3)(i) states:

> “The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer’s interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act.”

Section 1026.23(a)(3)(ii) defines “material disclosures” to mean:

> “the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g).”

**Analysis.**

**A. Ask 1 — the general rule.**
- The rescission period is measured from the **last** of three events: consummation; delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice; and delivery of all material disclosures. If the notice and disclosures are delivered before consummation, the period starts at consummation. If either is delivered after consummation, the period starts on the later delivery date.
- The period ends at **midnight of the third business day after** that last event. For rescission, “business day” is defined by § 1026.2(a)(6) as **all calendar days except Sundays and the federal legal public holidays specified in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a)**. Saturdays count. If the last day falls on a Sunday or a listed holiday, the period extends to the next day that is not a Sunday or listed holiday.
- Exercise is effective under § 1026.23(a)(2) when the consumer mails the written notice, files it for telegraphic transmission, or delivers it to the creditor’s designated place of business. A notice mailed by midnight on the last business day is therefore timely even if the creditor receives it later.
- “Material disclosures” are the items listed in § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii). If any required material disclosure is not delivered, the general rule’s last-event trigger has not been satisfied by that missing disclosure.
- If TILA § 125(f) applies because of a qualifying administrative proceeding, the rescission period is extended in accordance with that section.

**B. Ask 2 — the extended rule where notice or material disclosures are never delivered.**
- The second sentence of § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) applies when the required notice or the material disclosures are **not delivered**. In that case the right expires at the **first** of three events: **3 years after consummation**; **transfer of all of the consumer’s interest in the property**; or **sale of the property**.
- The three-year clock runs from **consummation**, not from the date the consumer discovers the violation, receives a demand, or first asserts rescission.
- A transfer of less than all of the consumer’s interest does not trigger the “transfer of all” clause. A sale of the property does trigger it, even if the sale occurs before the three-year date.
- If none of those events occurs earlier, the right ends at the three-year point. The three-year period is an outer limit on the right; it is not merely a statute of limitations for filing an action.
- A notice that does not satisfy § 1026.23(b), or a disclosure package that omits a required material disclosure, may not be the “required notice” or “all material disclosures” for purposes of starting the three-business-day period. Whether a particular document is compliant is a facts-specific question.

**C. Assumptions and caveats.**
- This answer assumes the transaction is a covered credit transaction under § 1026.23(a)(1) and is not exempt under § 1026.23(f) (for example, a residential mortgage transaction as defined in § 1026.2(a)(24), or certain refinancings or consolidations by the same creditor).
- This answer addresses the “never delivered” case in ask 2. Late delivery of the notice or material disclosures raises separate timing questions not presented here.
- State law may provide longer rescission rights or additional procedures; this answer addresses the federal Regulation Z rule only.
- Expiration of the right to rescind is distinct from any statute of limitations or procedural deadline for bringing a rescission claim in court.

**Bottom line.** For ask 1, the deadline is **midnight of the third business day following the last of consummation, delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice, or delivery of all material disclosures**. For ask 2, if the required notice or material disclosures are never delivered, the right expires at the **earliest of 3 years after consummation, transfer of all of the consumer’s interest in the property, or sale of the property**.

**Authority.** 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), (ii); § 1026.23(a)(2); § 1026.2(a)(6); see also 15 U.S.C. § 1635(a), (f); TILA § 125(f). Text reviewed against the current eCFR/GovInfo and CFPB Regulation Z sources.

quotes.whole:
§ 20.1201 Occupational dose limits for adults.




(a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.




(1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—




(i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or






(ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).








(2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:




(i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and






(ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.










(b) Doses received in excess of the annual limits, including doses received during accidents, emergencies, and planned special exposures, must be subtracted from the limits for planned special exposures that the individual may receive during the current year (see § 20.1206(e)(1)) and during the individual's lifetime (see § 20.1206(e)(2)).






(c) When the external exposure is determined by measurement with an external personal monitoring device, the deep-dose equivalent must be used in place of the effective dose equivalent, unless the effective dose equivalent is determined by a dosimetry method approved by the NRC. The assigned deep-dose equivalent must be for the part of the body receiving the highest exposure. The assigned shallow-dose equivalent must be the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure. The deep-dose equivalent, lens-dose equivalent, and shallow-dose equivalent may be assessed from surveys or other radiation measurements for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the occupational dose limits, if the individual monitoring device was not in the region of highest potential exposure, or the results of individual monitoring are unavailable.






(d) Derived air concentration (DAC) and annual limit on intake (ALI) values are presented in table 1 of appendix B to part 20 and may be used to determine the individual's dose (see § 20.2106) and to demonstrate compliance with the occupational dose limits.






(e) In addition to the annual dose limits, the licensee shall limit the soluble uranium intake by an individual to 10 milligrams in a week in consideration of chemical toxicity (see footnote 3 of appendix B to part 20).





(f) The licensee shall reduce the dose that an individual may be allowed to receive in the current year by the amount of occupational dose received while employed by any other person (see § 20.2104(e)).



[56 FR 23396, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 20185, Apr. 25, 1995; 63 FR 39482, July 23, 1998; 67 FR 16304, Apr. 5, 2002; 72 FR 68059, Dec. 4, 2007]

§ 20.1201 Occupational dose limits for adults.




(a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.




(1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—




(i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or






(ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).








(2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:




(i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and






(ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.










(b) Doses received in excess of the annual limits, including doses received during accidents, emergencies, and planned special exposures, must be subtracted from the limits for planned special exposures that the individual may receive during the current year (see § 20.1206(e)(1)) and during the individual's lifetime (see § 20.1206(e)(2)).






(c) When the external exposure is determined by measurement with an external personal monitoring device, the deep-dose equivalent must be used in place of the effective dose equivalent, unless the effective dose equivalent is determined by a dosimetry method approved by the NRC. The assigned deep-dose equivalent must be for the part of the body receiving the highest exposure. The assigned shallow-dose equivalent must be the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure. The deep-dose equivalent, lens-dose equivalent, and shallow-dose equivalent may be assessed from surveys or other radiation measurements for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the occupational dose limits, if the individual monitoring device was not in the region of highest potential exposure, or the results of individual monitoring are unavailable.






(d) Derived air concentration (DAC) and annual limit on intake (ALI) values are presented in table 1 of appendix B to part 20 and may be used to determine the individual's dose (see § 20.2106) and to demonstrate compliance with the occupational dose limits.






(e) In addition to the annual dose limits, the licensee shall limit the soluble uranium intake by an individual to 10 milligrams in a week in consideration of chemical toxicity (see footnote 3 of appendix B to part 20).





(f) The licensee shall reduce the dose that an individual may be allowed to receive in the current year by the amount of occupational dose received while employed by any other person (see § 20.2104(e)).

verdict.summary:
# Annual occupational dose limits for adult workers — 10 CFR § 20.1201(a)

## 1. Answer table (both units, as required)

| # | Quantity (regulatory term) | Citation | Limit in rem | Limit in Sv |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) — annual limit, the more limiting of (a)(1)(i) or (a)(1)(ii) | § 20.1201(a)(1)(i) | **5 rems** | **0.05 Sv** |
| 2 | Lens dose equivalent (lens of the eye) | § 20.1201(a)(2)(i) | **15 rems** | **0.15 Sv** |
| 3 | Shallow-dose equivalent to the skin of the whole body | § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii) | **50 rems** | **0.5 Sv** |

Unit conversion used throughout: 1 Sv = 100 rem, therefore rem x 0.01 = Sv. Check: 5 x 0.01 = 0.05; 15 x 0.01 = 0.15; 50 x 0.01 = 0.5. Each Sv figure above is identical to the figure printed in parentheses in the regulation itself, so no rounding discretion is introduced by this answer.

## 2. Regulatory text (verbatim, for verifiability)

> § 20.1201 Occupational dose limits for adults.
>
> (a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.
>
> (1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—
>
> (i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or
>
> (ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).
>
> (2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:
>
> (i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and
>
> (ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.
>
> [56 FR 23396, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 20185, Apr. 25, 1995; 63 FR 39482, July 23, 1998; 67 FR 16304, Apr. 5, 2002; 72 FR 68059, Dec. 4, 2007]

(The regulation writes "50 rem" in (a)(2)(ii); it means 50 rems, and the parenthetical 0.5 Sv confirms the magnitude.)

## 3. How each limit is to be applied (the part that makes the numbers usable)

**Ask 1 — total effective dose equivalent, 5 rems (0.05 Sv).** This is not a stand-alone number: § 20.1201(a)(1) sets the annual limit as *the more limiting of* two constraints — 5 rems TEDE, **or** 50 rems (0.5 Sv) for the sum of deep-dose equivalent plus committed dose equivalent to any single organ or tissue other than the lens. For a given worker you compute both and the lower governs. The 50 rems in (a)(1)(ii) is an **organ** constraint and is a different quantity from the 50 rems skin limit in (a)(2)(ii); they share a numeric value but are not interchangeable.

**Ask 2 — lens of the eye, 15 rems (0.15 Sv).** Applies as the lens dose equivalent, a separate limit outside the TEDE summation. § 20.1203 note is explicit: "The dose equivalents for the lens of the eye, the skin, and the extremities are not included in the summation, but are subject to separate limits." Do not roll lens dose into TEDE and do not compare lens dose against the 5 rem TEDE limit.

**Ask 3 — skin of the whole body, 50 rems (0.5 Sv).** This is the shallow-dose equivalent, and per § 20.1201(c) it must be "the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure" — not a whole-body average. The same 50 rem shallow-dose limit also applies to the skin of any extremity; that extremity provision is outside the three items asked but is stated in the same subparagraph and is normally quoted with it.

Supporting definitions (deep-dose equivalent, lens dose equivalent, shallow-dose equivalent, and the tissue weighting factors) are in § 20.1003; the 10 cm² averaging rule and the option to assess these quantities from surveys when the badge was not in the region of highest potential exposure are in § 20.1201(c).

## 4. Currency and verification

- Verified against: eCFR current title 10 § 20.1201 and Subpart C; GovInfo 2024 CFR vol. 1 (XML and PDF); GovInfo 2025 CFR vol. 1 Part 20 PDF. All three sources are word-for-word identical on the three figures.
- The section's amendment history ends at 72 FR 68059 (Dec. 4, 2007); no later amendment to these values appears in the 2024 or 2025 editions or in the current eCFR.
- **Not adopted — do not apply:** the ICRP 2011 recommendation of an equivalent dose limit of 20 mSv/year for the lens, and the 20 mSv lens limits used in IAEA BSS / EU law, have **not** been incorporated into 10 CFR Part 20. Under the U.S. NRC rule as published, the lens limit remains 15 rems (0.15 Sv). If a reader's procedure was written to 20 mSv, it is stricter than the CFR and must be cited to the licensee's own commitment, not to § 20.1201.
- Do not use the pre-1991 Part 20 quarterly lens limit (3 rems per quarter) — it was superseded by the 1991 revision cited above.

## 5. Adjacent provisions sometimes confused with § 20.1201(a) (stated so they are not mixed into the three answers)

| Population / situation | Provision | TEDE | Lens | Skin of whole body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adult worker (the ask) | § 20.1201(a) | 5 rem (0.05 Sv) | 15 rem (0.15 Sv) | 50 rem (0.5 Sv) |
| Miner (10% of adult limits) | § 20.1207 | 0.5 rem (5 mSv) | 1.5 rem (15 mSv) | 5 rem (50 mSv) |
| Embryo/fetus, entire gestation | § 20.1208(a) | 0.5 rem (5 mSv) | — | — |
| Planned special exposure ceiling | § 20.1206(e) | numerical values of § 20.1201(a) in any year; 5x annual limits per lifetime | same | same |

The miner and embryo/fetus figures are derived (10% of the adult values per the text of § 20.1207) and are offered only as context; they are not part of the answer to asks 1–3 and must not be quoted as § 20.1201(a) limits.

## 6. Suggested citation strings for compliance/training use

- "10 CFR § 20.1201(a)(1)(i) — total effective dose equivalent, 5 rems (0.05 Sv) per year."
- "10 CFR § 20.1201(a)(2)(i) — lens dose equivalent, 15 rems (0.15 Sv) per year."
- "10 CFR § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii) — shallow-dose equivalent to the skin of the whole body (averaged over the contiguous 10 cm² receiving the highest exposure), 50 rems (0.5 Sv) per year."

Editorial Note on Part 1926
Editorial Notes:

§ 1926.501 Duty to have fall protection.
(a) General.
(1) This section sets forth requirements for employers to provide fall protection systems. All fall protection required by this section shall conform to the criteria set forth in § 1926.502 of this subpart.
(2) The employer shall determine if the walking/working surfaces on which its employees are to work have the strength and structural integrity to support employees safely. Employees shall be allowed to work on those surfaces only when the surfaces have the requisite strength and structural integrity.
(b)
(1) Unprotected sides and edges.  Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.
(2) Leading edges.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1), 'Unprotected sides and edges' (federal OSHA construction standard, 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart M)

ASK 1 — Trigger height: 6 feet (1.8 m).
Each employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 6 feet (1.8 m) OR MORE above a lower level must be protected from falling. The threshold is inclusive: at exactly 6 ft 0 in the duty attaches. Below 6 ft, (b)(1) itself imposes no fall-protection duty (other paragraphs of § 1926.501 or other subparts may still apply — see Cautions).

ASK 2 — Systems that satisfy the duty: guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems. Exactly those three. The employer selects; the standard requires protection 'by the use of' one of them, and any system installed must meet the criteria in § 1926.502 (per § 1926.501(a)(1)).

1. GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim, § 1926.501(b)(1))

   "(b)(1) Unprotected sides and edges. Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."

   Source agreement (all four renderings carry identical (b)(1) wording):
   - eCFR current, 29 CFR 1926.501 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1926/subpart-M/section-1926.501
   - eCFR current, Subpart M — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/part-1926/subpart-M
   - GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 29 vol. 8, § 1926.501 (PDF) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title29-vol8/pdf/CFR-2025-title29-vol8-sec1926-501.pdf
   - GovInfo, CFR 2024 title 29 vol. 8, § 1926.501 (XML) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol8/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol8-sec1926-501.xml
   Because the 2024 and 2025 annual editions and the current eCFR point to the same text, the 6-ft trigger and the three named systems are stable across the versions checked; no amendment in that window changes either element.

2. WHAT THE PROVISION COVERS
   - 'Walking/working surface' is expressly parentheticaled as '(horizontal and vertical surface)' in the text, so the provision reaches vertical surfaces as well as floors, roofs, ramps and runways.
   - The duty runs to the employer; it is a duty to have protection in place, not a duty to train or warn. § 1926.501(a)(1) frames the whole section as 'requirements for employers to provide fall protection systems.'
   - § 1926.502(a)(2) (quoted in the fetched CFR 2025 text) requires the employer to 'provide and install all fall protection systems required by this subpart for an employee, and … comply with all other pertinent requirements of this subpart before that employee begins the work that necessitates the fall protection.' Fall protection is therefore a pre-task condition, not a progressive measure.
   - § 1926.501(a)(2) adds the separate predicate that the employer must determine the walking/working surface has the strength and structural integrity to support employees, and may allow work on it only if it does.

3. SYSTEM SELECTION — WHAT QUALIFIES AND WHAT DOES NOT, UNDER (b)(1)
   Qualifying (the only three named in (b)(1)):
   a. Guardrail systems — must meet § 1926.502(b). Representative criterion from the fetched text: top edge height of top rails, or equivalent members, 42 inches (1.1 m) ± 3 inches (8 cm) above the walking/working level (may exceed 45 in where conditions warrant and all other criteria are met). Note: 42 in is the guardrail member height, NOT the fall trigger height; the 6-ft trigger is measured from the working surface down to the lower level.
   b. Safety net systems — must meet § 1926.502(c).
   c. Personal fall arrest systems — must meet § 1926.502(d).
   The employer may use one system or a combination; nothing in (b)(1) ranks them or requires a specific one where any would work.

   NOT available under (b)(1) — these appear only in other paragraphs of Subpart M, and citing them against (b)(1) is a common compliance error:
   - Warning line systems, safety monitoring systems, and warning-line combinations — (b)(10) low-slope roofing only.
   - Controlled access zones — (b)(9) overhand bricklaying and related work.
   - Covers — (b)(4) holes (and (b)(7)(ii) excavations/wells/pits/shafts).
   - Positioning device systems — (b)(5) formwork and reinforcing steel.
   - Fences and barricades — (b)(7)(ii) excavations.
   - A fall protection plan under § 1926.502(k) in lieu of systems — the presumption/burden note in the regulation attaches to the paragraph that authorizes it (it appears immediately before paragraph (b)(14) in the current text, i.e., it belongs to the residential-construction paragraph (b)(13)); (b)(1) contains no such exception and no infeasibility escape hatch. Do not substitute a plan for (b)(1) protection.

4. APPLYING IT ON A SITE — procedure
   Step 1. Identify each walking/working surface and every side or edge of it.
   Step 2. Determine whether the side or edge is 'unprotected.' The term is a defined term in § 1926.500(b); the definition text was NOT among the passages retrieved for this answer, so verify it against the current § 1926.500(b) before relying on a specific dimension (commonly cited as no wall or guardrail at least 39 in high, but treat that figure as unverified here).
   Step 3. Measure vertically from the working surface to the 'lower level' to which an employee could fall. Also a defined term in § 1926.500(b) — verify the text; do not assume it means only grade.
   Step 4. If the measured height is 6 ft (1.8 m) or more, select one of the three systems, design/install it to the applicable § 1926.502 criteria, and complete installation before the employee begins the work that creates the exposure (§ 1926.502(a)(2)).
   Step 5. Document the selection, the installation inspection, and (for personal fall arrest) the anchorage, clearance and rescue provisions required by § 1926.502(d).
   Step 6. If the height is under 6 ft, close out (b)(1) — but re-screen against (b)(8)(i) (employee less than 6 ft above dangerous equipment must still be protected by guardrail systems or equipment guards) and against any other applicable subpart.

5. CAUTIONS / BOUNDARIES OF THIS ANSWER
   - Jurisdiction. This is the federal OSHA construction requirement. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective but may use different wording, different triggers, or additional systems; in a State Plan jurisdiction, check the state rule before finalizing. (State-plan content was not retrieved.)
   - Standard/industry. This is 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M (construction). The general-industry walking-working-surfaces rule (29 CFR 1910.28/1910.29) uses a different trigger and is outside the sources verified here.
   - Scope exclusions. § 1926.500(a)(2) removes certain operations from Subpart M; the exclusion list was not among the retrieved passages. Confirm applicability for the specific operation before citing (b)(1).
   - Other paragraphs of § 1926.501 carry their own system lists and, in some cases, their own triggers — e.g., (b)(4) holes more than 6 ft (personal fall arrest, covers, or guardrails); (b)(6) ramps/runways/walkways 6 ft or more (guardrail systems); (b)(9)(ii) reaching more than 10 in below the working surface (guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest); (b)(14) wall openings (guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest). Where an operation fits a specific paragraph, that paragraph — not (b)(1) — controls, with (b)(15) as the residual catch-all for walking/working surfaces not otherwise addressed.
   - Currency. Verified against eCFR 'current' and the 2024 and 2025 CFR annual editions as of retrieval; re-verify before relying on this in an enforcement or litigation posture.

4.—(1) Subject to regulation 5, a worker’s working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days.
(2) An employer shall take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect the health and safety of workers, to ensure that the limit specified in paragraph (1) is complied with in the case of each worker employed by him in relation to whom it applies.
(3) Subject to paragraphs (4) and (5) and any agreement under regulation 23(b), the reference periods which apply in the case of a worker are—
(a)where a relevant agreement provides for the application of this regulation in relation to successive periods of 17 weeks, each such period, or
(b)in any other case, any period of 17 weeks in the course of his employment.
(4) Where a worker has worked for his employer for less than 17 weeks, the reference period applicable in his case is the period that has elapsed since he started work for his employer.

verdict.summary:
Legal position under regulation 4(1) of the Working Time Regulations 1998 (general information, not advice on a specific worker's situation).

1. The limit. Regulation 4(1) provides that, unless the employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work, a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period applicable to the worker shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days. The 48 hours is an average, not an absolute cap on any particular week: a worker may work more than 48 hours in a given week provided the average over the applicable reference period remains at or below 48 hours per seven days. Overtime hours count towards the average.

2. Reference period and calculation. The default reference period is 17 weeks. It may be a succession of 17-week periods where a relevant agreement so provides; otherwise it is any period of 17 weeks in the course of employment. If the worker has been employed for less than 17 weeks, the reference period is the period since starting work. For workers excluded from certain provisions by regulation 21, the 17-week references become 26 weeks. Under reg 4(6) the average is calculated as (A + B) / C, where A is the aggregate number of working hours in the reference period, B is the aggregate number of working hours in the period immediately after the reference period ending when the number of days worked equals the number of excluded days in the reference period, and C is the number of weeks in the reference period. Excluded days include annual leave under regulation 13, 13A or 15B, sick leave, maternity, paternity, adoption or parental leave, and days when the reg 4(1) limit did not apply because of the written opt-out.

3. How a worker is taken outside the limit. The route in reg 4(1) is the individual opt-out: the employer must first obtain the worker's agreement in writing to perform work to which the limit would otherwise apply. It must be obtained before the work is performed; a purported retrospective agreement does not satisfy reg 4(1). The agreement may be for a specified or indefinite period and may be terminated by the worker on notice under regulation 5. The employer must keep up-to-date records of workers who carry out work to which the limit does not apply because of such an agreement (reg 4(2)). The opt-out is individual, not a collective agreement, and it does not disapply other working time protections, such as night-work limits, rest periods, annual leave, or the separate 40-hour average limit for young workers. Certain categories are excluded from the 48-hour limit by other provisions of the Regulations, but that is a separate route from the individual written opt-out.

4. Consequence. If there is no valid written opt-out and the average exceeds 48 hours per seven days over the applicable reference period, the employer is in breach of reg 4(1); reg 4(2) also requires the employer to take all reasonable steps to secure compliance.

quotes.question_text: In NIST SP 800-63B-4, what minimum length must verifiers require for a password used as a single-factor authentication mechanism, what minimum for a password used only as part of multi-factor authentication, and what maximum length should they permit at least?
quotes.text:
Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length. Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length.
Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters.

quotes.whole:
Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length. Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length.
Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters.
Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD accept all printing ASCII [RFC20] characters and the space character in passwords.
Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD accept Unicode [ISO/ISC 10646] characters in passwords. Each Unicode code point SHALL be counted as a single character when evaluating password length.
Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT impose other composition rules (e.g., requiring mixtures of different character types) for passwords.
Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT require subscribers to change passwords periodically. However, verifiers SHALL force a change if there is evidence that the authenticator has been compromised.
Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT permit the subscriber to store a hint (e.g., a reminder of how the password was created) that is accessible to an unauthenticated claimant.

quotes.whole:
To help the claimant successfully enter a password, the verifier SHOULD offer an option to display the password — rather than a series of dots or asterisks — while it is entered and until it is submitted to the verifier. This allows the claimant to confirm their entry if they are in a location where their screen is unlikely to be observed. The verifier MAY also permit the claimant’s device to display individual entered characters for a short time after each character is typed to verify the correct entry. This is common on mobile devices.
Verifiers MAY make limited allowances for mistyping (e.g., removing leading and trailing whitespace characters before verification, allowing the verification of passwords with differing cases for the leading character) if the password remains at least the required minimum length after such processing and the complexity of the resulting password is not significantly reduced.
Verifiers and CSPs SHALL use approved encryption and an authenticated protected channel when requesting passwords.

Multi-factor out-of-band authenticators operate similarly to single-factor out-of-band authenticators (see Sec. 3.1.3.1). However, they require the presentation and verification of an activation factor (i.e., a password or a biometric characteristic) before allowing the claimant to complete the authentication transaction (i.e., before accessing or entering the authentication secret as appropriate for the authentication flow being used). A biometric activation factor SHALL meet the requirements of Sec. 3.2.3, including limits on the number of consecutive authentication failures. The password or biometric sample used for activation and any biometric data derived from the biometric sample (e.g., a fingerprint image and feature locations produced by a fingerprint feature extractor) SHALL be erased immediately after an authentication operation.

quotes.whole:
2.2.1. Permitted Authenticator Types
At AAL2, authentication SHALL  use either a multi-factor authenticator or a combination
of two separate authentication factors. A multi-factor authenticator requires two factors
to execute a single authentication event, such as a cryptographically secure device with
an integrated biometric sensor that is required to activate the device. Authenticator
requirements are specified in Sec. 3.
When a multi-factor authenticator is used, any of the following MAY  be used:
• Multi-factor out-of-band authenticator (Sec. 3.1.3.4)
• Multi-factor OTP (Sec. 3.1.5)
• Multi-factor cryptographic authentication (Sec. 3.1.7)
When a combination of two single-factor authenticators is used, the combination SHALL
include one physical authenticator (i.e., “something you have”) from the following list in
conjunction with either a password (Sec. 3.1.1) or a biometric comparison:
• Look-up secret (Sec. 3.1.2)

This guideline focuses on the authentication of subjects who interact with government information systems over networks to establish that a given claimant is a subscriber who has been previously authenticated. The result of the authentication process may be used locally by the system performing the authentication or asserted elsewhere in a federated identity system. This document defines technical requirements for each of the three authentication assurance levels. verdict.summary:
# SP 800-63B-4 passord length requirements — answer and implementation spec

Source of record: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management, July 2025). The three numbers below were read verbatim from two independently fetched copies of the publication — the NIST pages HTML rendering (`pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/`) and the NIST PDF (`tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=959882`) — which agree word-for-word, and are corroborated by the NIST SP 800-63-4 Implementation Resources FAQ.

## 1. The answer

| # | Question | Requirement level | Value |
|---|----------|-------------------|-------|
| 1 | Minimum length for a passord used as a **single-factor** authentication mechanism | **SHALL** | **15 characters** |
| 2 | Minimum length for a passord used **only as part of multi-factor** authentication | **SHALL** (when the shorter allowance is taken) | **8 characters** |
| 3 | Maximum passord length verifiers **SHOULD permit at least** | **SHOULD** | **64 characters** |

Verbatim normative text (identical in both fetched copies):

> "Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length. Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length.
>
> Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters."

Citation: the numbered passord-requirement list in Sec. 3.1.1 (Passwords) of SP 800-63B-4, items 1 and 2. (The fetched excerpt shows the list but not the sub-section label; confirm the sub-section number against the published PDF before using it in a formal compliance filing.)

## 2. How to read the modal verbs (this is where most implementations go wrong)

- **15 is a floor that is mandatory.** A verifier that accepts a 14-character single-factor passord is non-compliant. There is no risk-based exception in this clause.
- **8 is a *permitted relaxation*, not a mandate.** The clause says verifiers *MAY* allow MFA-only passords to be shorter, but if they do, the floor is 8. A verifier that requires 15 characters for *every* passord — including MFA-only ones — is fully compliant. Do not implement "MFA passords MUST be 8"; implement "MFA passords MUST be ≥ 8, and MAY be required to be ≥ 15."
- **The 8-character allowance applies only to passords that are *only* used as part of MFA.** The moment the same passord can also be used alone (e.g., the same secret authenticates at AAL1, or is reused as a single-factor credential), it falls under the 15-character rule. This is a per-credential property, not a per-user or per-system property; it must be tracked on the credential record.
- **64 is a cap on *rejection*, not on acceptance.** "SHOULD permit a maximum length of at least 64" means the verifier must **accept** passords of at least 64 characters. A verifier that refuses or truncates a 65-character passord is non-compliant with the intent; a verifier that accepts 256 characters is fine. "SHOULD" is a recommendation, but NIST's rationale is explicit elsewhere in the document (denial-of-service and passord-manager compatibility), and a verifier that caps below 64 both contradicts the guidance and breaks passord managers.

## 3. Revision delta — do not regress to Rev 3

SP 800-63B-3 required a minimum of **8** characters for memorized secrets used as a single factor. Rev 4 raises the single-factor floor to **15**. The NIST FAQ states this directly:

> "Minimum password length of 15 characters for passwords being used as a single authentication factor at AAL1 (increased from 8 characters)."

Any verifier, checklist, or test suite built from Rev 3 that asserts "8 is acceptable for a single factor" must be updated; it is now a finding. Note the collision hazard: **8 now means "MFA-only floor"**, not "single-factor floor" — the same digit that was the Rev-3 answer is now the Rev-4 answer to a *different* question. Call this out in code comments and in review guidance, or reviewers will sign off the wrong thing.

## 4. Adjacent requirements that constrain the same code path

The following come from the same requirements list and must be implemented in the same validator, or the length floors are trivially bypassable or violate the user:

- **SHALL NOT impose other composition rules** (no character-class requirements, no special-character mandates). Complexity rules must be *deleted*, not merely discouraged — Rev 3 merely discouraged them.
- **SHALL NOT require periodic passord change** (force a change only on evidence of compromation).
- **SHALL NOT permit a passord hint accessible to an unauthenticated claimant.**
- **SHOULD accept all printing ASCII (RFC 20) characters and the space character**; **SHOULD accept Unicode (ISO/IEC 10646) characters**, and **each Unicode code point SHALL count as a single character** when evaluating length. Do not count UTF-8 bytes or UTF-16 code units — that would let a 5-emoji passord pass a 15-character check, and would also make the 64-character acceptance ceiling wrong.
- **Mistyping allowances are bounded**: removing leading/trailing whitespace or case-folding the leading character is permitted *only if the passord still meets the required minimum after such processing*.
- **Not in the fetched excerpt, verify before relying on it:** passord blocklist screening (commonly-used / compromised passords) and rate limiting. They exist in SP 800-63B-4 but were not part of the extracted text; do not quote a modal verb for them from this document.

### Distinguish "activation secrets" — a different category with a different number

SP 800-63B-4 introduces **activation factors** verified locally on the authenticator/endpoint (e.g., a phone PIN unlocking a key). Per the NIST FAQ, activation secrets are required to be **at least 4 characters** and encouraged to be at least 6, with a limit of 10 consecutive failures. **4 and 6 are NOT answers to ask 2.** They apply only to locally verified activation secrets, not to a passord verified by the verifier as part of MFA. Keep these in separate constants and separate code paths; confusing them silently lowers the MFA floor from 8 to 4.

## 5. Implementation spec

### Constants

```
PASSWORD_MIN_SINGLE_FACTOR   = 15   // SHALL — no exception
PASSWORD_MIN_MFA_ONLY        = 8    // SHALL when the shorter allowance is taken; MAO may keep 15
PASSWORD_MAX_ACCEPT_MINIMUM  = 64   // SHOULD — verifier must accept at least this many
ACTIVATION_SECRET_MIN        = 4    // separate category, locally verified only
ACTIVATION_SECRET_RECOMENDED = 6
// NO maximum-length cap below 64. Prefer no cap at all, or a high operational cap (e.g., 1024).
```

### Validator pseudocode

```
function validateNewPassword(rawInput, credentialUse):
    // credentialUse ∈ {SINGLE_FACTOR, MFA_ONLY}

    // 1. Canonicalise only in the ways the guideline permits.
    candidate = normalizeUnicode(rawInput)          // NFKC or none; must not expand length arbitrarilly
    candidate = stripLeadingAndTrailingWhitespace(candidate)

    // 2. Length in CODE POINTS, not bytes and not UTF-16 units.
    n = countUnicodeCodePoints(candidate)

    // 3. Floor.
    floor = (credentialUse == SNGLE_FACTOR) ? 15 : 8
    if n < floor:
        reject("Passord must be at least " + floor + " characters.")

    // 4. Acceptance ceiling: NEVER reject merely for length up to at least 64.
    if n > HARD_MAX_ACCEPTED and HARD_MAX_ACCEPTED < 64:
        // this is a build-time assertion failure, not a runtime branch
        assert(false, "Configured maximum is below the 64-character SHOULD.")
    // Do NOT truncate the input to 64 (or any other value) before hashing.

    // 5. No composition rules.
    //    Do NOT check for uppercase/digit/symbol presence. Do NOT block spaces.

    // 6. Store with a memory-hard hash; if a verifier-side pepper is used,
    //    keep it separate from the hash store.
    store(credential, hash(candidate))

// Build-time invariant, run in CI:
assert(HARD_MAX_ACCEPTED >= 64)
assert(PASSWORD_MIN_SNGLE_FACTOR > PASSWORD_MIN_MFA_ONLY)   // 15 > 8
assert(PASSWORD_MIN_MFA_ONLY >= ACTIVATION_SECRET_MIN)      // 8 > 4
```

### Boundary test matrix (must all pass)

| Test | Input | Context | Expected |
|------|-------|---------|----------|
| T1 | 14 ASCII chars | single factor | **reject** |
| T2 | 15 ASCII chars | single factor | **accept** |
| T3 | 7 ASCII chars | MFA only | **reject** |
| T4 | 8 ASCII chars | MFA only | **accept** |
| T5 | 8 ASCII chars | single factor | **reject** (a MFA-only passord promoted to single-factor use must be re-screened) |
| T6 | 64 ASCII chars | either | **accept** |
| T7 | 200 ASCII chars | either | **accept**, and the stored hash must reflect all 200 (no truncation) |
| T8 | 15 emoji | single factor | **accept** (15 code points, even though UTF-8 length is 60 bytes) |
| T9 | 14 emoji | single factor | **reject** (code-point count, not byte count) |
| T10 | "correct horse battery staple" (28 chars, spaces) | single factor | **accept** (spaces are accepted; no composition rules) |
| T11 | "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" (16 chars, one class) | single factor | **accept** (no composition rules) |
| T12 | "  shortpassord  " (12 after trim) | single factor | **reject** (mispelling allowance may not drop below the floor) |
| T13 | 6-digit PIN on authenticator | activation secret | **accept** (different constant, 4/6 rule) |
| T14 | 3-digit PIN on authenticator | activation secret | **reject** |

## 6. Compliance-review checklist (what a reviewer should ask for)

1. Show the configured minimum for single-factor credentials — must be ≥ 15.
2. Show the configured minimum for MFA-only credentials — must be ≥ 8, and the code must not be able to assign a credential to the MFA-only bucket unless that credential is provably never usable alone.
3. Show that the maximum accepted length is ≥ 64 and that no truncation occurs before hashing.
4. Show that length is computed in Unicode code points.
5. Show that composition rules and periodic-expiry rules have been *removed*, not disabled by default.
6. Show that activation-secret constants (4/6) are separate and cannot be applied to verifier-checked passords.
7. Grep for any Rev-3-era assertion of "8 is fine for single factor" — each instance is a finding.

## 7. Residual uncertainty

None on the three values: they appear verbatim in two independently fetched copies of the publication and are corroborated by the NIST FAQ. The only unverified detail is the precise sub-section number of the requirements list and the exact wording of the blocklist/rate-limiting clauses, both flagged above for confirmation against the published PDF.

At AAL2, authentication SHALL use either a multi-factor authenticator or a combination of two separate authentication factors. verdict.summary:
REGULATORY ANSWER — 14 CFR § 91.151(a), Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions (airplanes)

1. THE REQUIREMENT (verbatim, current eCFR and GPO CFR text, identical in both sources)

"§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.
(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

2. ANSWER TO ASK 1 — fuel beyond the first point of intended landing, airplane, VFR

  Day   : 30 minutes at normal cruising speed (minimum)
  Night : 45 minutes at normal cruising speed (minimum)

Both figures are expressed by the regulation itself as time, so no conversion is required to state them. They are stated "assuming normal cruising speed," i.e., the reserve time is converted to a fuel quantity using the airplane's normal cruise fuel flow, not its climb or maximum-power flow.

3. ANSWER TO ASK 2 — each as a time at normal cruising speed

The regulation supplies the time directly; the pilot supplies "normal cruising speed." The operational form of the rule is therefore:

  Required fuel on board at brake release =
      (fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather)
    + (normal cruise fuel flow x 0.50 h)   [day]
    + (normal cruise fuel flow x 0.75 h)   [night]

Equivalent distance form (useful for a quick cross-check at the planning stage):

  Day   : 0.50 x normal cruising TAS
  Night : 0.75 x normal cruising TAS

  At 110 KTAS normal cruise: day reserve = 55 NM; night reserve = 90 NM is wrong -> recompute: 0.75 x 110 = 82.5 NM. (Corrected values: day 55 NM, night 82.5 NM.)
  At 120 KTAS normal cruise: day reserve = 60 NM; night reserve = 90 NM.

Fuel-quantity form, worked at a representative normal cruise burn of 10.0 gal/h:

  Day   : 0.50 h x 10.0 gal/h = 5.0 gal
  Night : 0.75 h x 10.0 gal/h = 7.5 gal

(For reference only, and NOT applicable to airplanes: the rotorcraft figure in § 91.151(b) is 20 minutes, which at 10.0 gal/h would be 3.3 gal / 40 NM at 120 KTAS. Do not apply this to airplanes.)

4. SCOPE NOTES A REGULATORY SPECIALIST SHOULD ATTACH

(a) Airplane vs. rotorcraft. § 91.151(a) governs airplanes; § 91.151(b) governs rotorcraft and imposes 20 minutes, with no day/night split. The 30/45-minute figures do not apply to helicopters, and the 20-minute figure does not apply to airplanes.

(b) No alternate-airport fuel under VFR. Unlike the IFR rule, § 91.167(a)(2), § 91.151 contains no requirement to carry fuel to a destination alternate. The VFR reserve is strictly: fuel to the first point of intended landing, plus 30 (day) or 45 (night) minutes thereafter. If an alternate is in fact used, fuel to reach it is part of the fuel to the first point of intended landing (or the flight must otherwise be planned to land with the reserve intact).

(c) The wind/weather qualifier is part of the rule. The fuel to the first point of intended landing must be computed "considering wind and forecast weather conditions" — i.e., headwind component and forecast conditions on the planned route, not still-air distance.

(d) These are regulatory minimums, not planning targets. More restrictive requirements may control: an operator's OpSpecs or a Part 135/121 rule, an Airplane Flight Manual limitation, or § 91.3 (pilot in command's emergency authority and responsibility). Where a more restrictive requirement applies, it governs.

(e) "Day" and "night" track the § 1.1 definitions (night = the period from the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time). The reserve bracket is determined by the condition in which the flight is conducted; a flight that will be in the air at night is planned to the night figure. When in doubt, plan to the 45-minute figure.

(f) Fuel must be usable. The reserve is measured in fuel that can actually be used in flight; the airplane must also be operated within its AFM fuel and weight limits.

5. ONE-LINE DELIVERABLE

Under 14 CFR § 91.151(a), an airplane beginning a VFR flight must carry, beyond fuel to reach the first point of intended landing, enough fuel to fly 30 minutes at normal cruising speed by day and 45 minutes at normal cruising speed at night.

quotes.whole:
§ 164.404 Notification to individuals.
(a) Standard —
(1) General rule.  A covered entity shall, following the discovery of a breach of unsecured protected health information, notify each individual whose unsecured protected health information has been, or is reasonably believed by the covered entity to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed as a result of such breach.
(2) Breaches treated as discovered.  For purposes of paragraph (a)(1) of this section, §§ 164.406(a), and 164.408(a), a breach shall be treated as discovered by a covered entity as of the first day on which such breach is known to the covered entity, or, by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known to the covered entity. A covered entity shall be deemed to have knowledge of a breach if such breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is a workforce member or agent of the covered entity (determined in accordance with the federal common law of agency).

verdict.summary:
# Deadline for individual breach notification — 45 CFR § 164.404(b)

## Short answer

A covered entity must notify an affected individual **without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of the breach**. The 60-day period runs from **discovery of the breach**, where discovery is defined by § 164.404(a)(2) as the first day the breach is known to the covered entity or, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known.

- **Standard:** notification "without unreasonable delay" (a conduct obligation — notice may be due well before day 60).
- **Outer limit:** 60 calendar days after discovery — a hard ceiling, not a target and not a default.
- **Trigger event:** discovery of the breach (actual or constructive/deemed discovery), not the date of the breach itself, not the date the investigation closes, and not the date the risk assessment is completed.

## Governing text (as published, current through the 2025 CFR revision)

45 CFR § 164.404(b), *Implementation specification: Timeliness of notification*:

> “Except as provided in § 164.412, a covered entity shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.”

45 CFR § 164.404(a)(2), *Breaches treated as discovered*:

> “For purposes of paragraph (a)(1) of this section, §§ 164.406(a), and 164.408(a), a breach shall be treated as discovered by a covered entity as of the first day on which such breach is known to the covered entity, or, by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known to the covered entity. A covered entity shall be deemed to have knowledge of a breach if such breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is a workforce member or agent of the covered entity (determined in accordance with the federal common law of agency).”

Source verification: identical text retrieved from eCFR (45 CFR subtitle A, subchapter C, part 164, subpart D, § 164.404) and from the 2025 print CFR (title 45, vol. 2, § 164.404, GovInfo). No amendment altering the 60-day figure or the discovery trigger was found; the section's source note reads “[74 FR 42767, Aug. 24, 2009, as amended at 78 FR 5695, Jan. 25, 2013]”.

## What the trigger event means in practice

1. **Actual knowledge.** The clock starts the first day any workforce member or agent of the covered entity (other than the person committing the breach) knows of the breach. Knowledge is imputed — it does not wait for the privacy officer to be told.
2. **Constructive knowledge.** The clock also starts the first day the breach would have been known by exercising reasonable diligence. An unreviewed audit log or an unopened incident queue does not hold the clock back.
3. **Not the breach date.** If a laptop was stolen on 1 June and the theft was discovered on 20 June, the 60 days run from 20 June.
4. **Not the end of the investigation.** The risk assessment that determines whether a breach is reportable should be completed promptly, but the notification deadline is measured from discovery, not from the completion of that assessment.

## Counting the 60 days

- Count in **calendar days**, not business days. Weekends and federal holidays are included.
- There is **no extension** for weekends, holidays, or the difficulty of drafting the notice.
- Treat the day of discovery as **day 0**; the 60th calendar day after discovery is the outer limit.
- Worked example: breach discovered **Monday, 3 March 2025** → day 0 = 3 March; day 28 = 31 March; day 58 = 30 April; day 59 = 1 May; **day 60 = Friday, 2 May 2025**. Notice must be *provided* (sent) by 2 May 2025 — and earlier if delay would be unreasonable.

## The one stated exception

Section 164.404(b) opens with “Except as provided in § 164.412” (law enforcement delay). Where a law enforcement official provides the written statement described in § 164.412, notification otherwise required by § 164.404 is delayed for the period specified. This is the only carve-out appearing in the text of § 164.404(b) itself; it suspends the obligation rather than creating a general extension of the 60-day period, and it should be documented in the breach file if relied upon.

## Scope notes

- **In scope:** notification to the affected individual(s) under § 164.404 only.
- **Out of scope (different provisions, do not conflate with the 60-day individual clock):** media notification for breaches affecting more than 500 residents of a State or jurisdiction (§ 164.406, also 60 calendar days from discovery); notification to the Secretary (§ 164.408); business associate notification to the covered entity (§ 164.414(b), separately 60 calendar days from the business associate's discovery).
- **Content of the notice** is governed by § 164.404(c) and is not part of this answer.

## Compliance control points (recordkeeping and defensibility)

- Log the **date of discovery** on the day it occurs, with the basis (who knew, when, and how the knowledge arose). That date, not the incident date, is what an examiner will test.
- Log the **date the notice was sent**, per individual, with the delivery method — including substitute notice under § 164.404(d)(2) where contact information is insufficient or out of date (conspicuous website posting for 90 days or major-media notice, plus a toll-free number active at least 90 days, where 10 or more individuals are affected).
- Retain the notice, the discovery log, the risk assessment, and the send records for **6 years** from the date of creation or the date last in effect, per § 164.530(j).
- Escalation rule: if day 45 passes without notice being sent, treat it as a reportable control failure and escalate — the standard, not the ceiling, is the operative obligation.

verdict.summary:
## Authority and scope

47 CFR § 97.313, current eCFR text (fetched 2026-11-17), consistent with the GPO 2024 edition of 47 CFR part 97, subpart D. This answer is limited to the two limits asked for; § 97.313 also contains other band-, mode-, and licensee-specific limits that are outside this question.

## Findings

| Ask | Provision | Regulatory limit | Unit and measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. General maximum transmitter power for an amateur station | § 97.313(b) | **1.5 kW PEP** (equivalent to 1500 W PEP) | Unit: kW. Measure: peak envelope power (PEP) of the transmitter. |
| 2. Lower maximum on the 10.10–10.15 MHz segment | § 97.313(c)(1) | **200 W PEP** (equivalent to 0.2 kW PEP) | Unit: W. Measure: transmitter power output, peak envelope power (PEP). |

## Regulatory text relied on

§ 97.313(b):

> “No station may transmit with a transmitter power exceeding 1.5 kW PEP.”

§ 97.313(c), opening text and paragraph (c)(1):

> “No station may transmit with a transmitter power output exceeding 200 W PEP:
> (1) On the 10.10-10.15 MHz segment;”

## Application and compliance notes

1. **General ceiling:** The general maximum transmitter power for an amateur station under § 97.313(b) is **1.5 kW PEP**. This is an absolute ceiling, not an operating target.
2. **10.10–10.15 MHz segment:** The more restrictive limit in § 97.313(c)(1) is **200 W PEP transmitter power output**. On that segment, 200 W PEP controls; the general 1.5 kW PEP ceiling does not authorize higher power there. Numerically, 200 W is below 1500 W, so the two stated values are consistent.
3. **Minimum-power duty:** § 97.313(a) independently requires an amateur station to “use the minimum transmitter power necessary to carry out the desired communications.” Thus 1.5 kW PEP and 200 W PEP are upper limits only; operation must not exceed them and must also use no more power than necessary.
4. **Measure:** Both limits are expressed in **PEP — peak envelope power**. Paragraph (b) uses the phrase “transmitter power,” while paragraph (c) uses “transmitter power output”; both are stated in PEP. Do not substitute average power, carrier power, or DC input power for these limits unless another rule specifically requires a different measure.

§ 173.120 Class 3—Definitions.
(a) Flammable liquid.  For the purpose of this subchapter, a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions:
(1) Any liquid meeting one of the definitions specified in § 173.115.
(2) Any mixture having one or more components with a flash point of 60 °C (140 °F) or higher, that make up at least 99 percent of the total volume of the mixture, if the mixture is not offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point.
(3) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) that does not sustain combustion according to ASTM D 4206 (IBR, see § 171.7 of this subchapter) or the procedure in appendix H of this part.
(4) Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) and with a fire point greater than 100 °C (212 °F) according to ISO 2592 (IBR, see § 171.7 of this subchapter).
