verdict.summary:
# SMTP line-length limits under RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1

## 1. Direct answer

| Line type | Max total length | Clause | What the count includes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Text line** | **1000 octets** | RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.6 | The entire line **including the terminating `<CRLF>`** (2 octets). The duplicated leading dot used for transparency is **not** counted. |
| **Reply line** | **512 octets** | RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.5 | The entire line **including the 3-digit reply code, the `-`/`<SP>` separator, the reply text, and the terminating `<CRLF>`**. |
| Command line (for contrast) | 512 octets | §4.5.3.1.4 | The command word, parameters, and the `<CRLF>`. |

So: **1000 octets for a text line, 512 octets for a reply line, both counted in octets, both inclusive of the terminating CRLF**; the reply-line count additionally includes the reply code.

## 2. Verbatim source text

RFC 5321, §4.5.3.1.5 and §4.5.3.1.6 (identical at rfc-editor.org, datatracker.ietf.org, and both mirrors consulted):

> **4.5.3.1.5. Reply Line**
>
> The maximum total length of a reply line including the reply code and
> the <CRLF> is 512 octets.  More information may be conveyed through
> multiple-line replies.
>
> **4.5.3.1.6. Text Line**
>
> The maximum total length of a text line including the <CRLF> is 1000
> octets (not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency).
> This number may be increased by the use of SMTP Service Extensions.

And the unit statement from the §4.5.3 preamble:

> ... in octets where absolute lengths, rather than character counts, are intended.

For contrast, §4.5.3.1.4:

> The maximum total length of a command line including the command word
> and the <CRLF> is 512 octets.  SMTP extensions may be used to
> increase this limit.

The `emailcore` revision draft (draft-ietf-emailcore-rfc5321bis-14) reproduces all three clauses with the same numbers, so the figures are stable across the base spec and its revision.

## 3. What the counts include — in detail

**Both limits are counted in octets (8-bit bytes), not characters.** Any multi-byte encoding counts every byte. Under SMTPUTF8 (RFC 6531), a 500-character UTF-8 line of 3-byte characters is 1500 octets and is over the limit even though it looks short. Do not size buffers in characters.

**Text line (1000 octets), §4.5.3.1.6:**
- Includes the terminating `<CRLF>` — the two octets `0x0D 0x0A` are part of the 1000.
- Therefore at most **998 octets of line content** (text + any leading dot that is part of the data) fit per line.
- Explicitly **excludes** the extra leading dot added for dot-stuffing transparency. A content line beginning with `.` is transmitted as `..`; that duplicated dot is outside the count, so a maximally stuffed line occupies **1 + 998 + 2 = 1001 octets on the wire** while still conforming. This is the one place where an on-the-wire octet count legitimately exceeds the stated 1000.
- Applies to message content lines (header and body) and, generally, to any line of text in the protocol that is not a command or reply.
- May be **increased by SMTP Service Extensions** (stated in the clause itself).

**Reply line (512 octets), §4.5.3.1.5:**
- Includes the **reply code** (3 digits, e.g. `250`).
- Includes the separator that follows it — `<SP>` on the final line, `-` on continuation lines.
- Includes the reply text. Note §4.2: "The space (blank) following the reply code is considered part of the text."
- Includes the terminating `<CRLF>`.
- Budget: 3 (code) + 1 (separator) + **506 octets of text** + 2 (CRLF) = 512.
- The limit is **per line**. A multi-line reply is not bounded at 512 octets in total; §4.5.3.1.5 says "More information may be conveyed through multiple-line replies," so each continuation line carries its own 512-octet budget.

**Command line (512 octets), §4.5.3.1.4** — quoted because readers routinely conflate it with the text-line limit: it is 512, not 1000, and includes the command word and the `<CRLF>`.

## 4. Why the two numbers differ (the part that is usually misremembered)

- **1000** is the *text line* limit — content carried over the wire as message text.
- **512** applies to *command lines* and *reply lines* — the protocol dialogue itself.
- A common error is to state "SMTP lines are 512 bytes"; that is true only of command and reply lines. Message text lines get 1000.
- A second common error is to state "512/1000 characters"; the RFC says octets.
- A third is to exclude the CRLF from the count. Both clauses say "including the `<CRLF>`".

## 5. Verification checklist (for anyone applying this)

1. Measure the line **as transmitted**, including the terminating `<CRLF>`, in **octets**.
2. For text lines: assert `len(line_including_crlf) <= 1000`, with the dot-stuffing dot excluded from the measurement. Content-only budget: 998.
3. For reply lines: assert `len(reply_line_including_crlf) <= 512`, counting the 3-digit code and the separator. Text-only budget: 506.
4. For command lines: assert `len(command_line_including_crlf) <= 512`.
5. Never assume an extension is absent: §4.5.3.1.6 and §4.5.3.1.4 both state that SMTP Service Extensions may raise these limits, so a receiver should not treat 1000/512 as a hard rejection threshold without checking the negotiated extension set.

## 6. Sources

- RFC 5321, *Simple Mail Transfer Protocol*, J. Klensin, October 2008 — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321.html (§4.5.3.1.4–§4.5.3.1.6; fetched 2026-11-17T05:41:05Z, sha256 5df422fb9940)
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5321.html (fetched 2026-11-17T05:41:06Z, sha256 4969a8357d61)
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-emailcore-rfc5321bis-14 (fetched 2026-11-17T05:41:06Z, sha256 478ff622a6ad) — reproduces the same limits
- https://www.hjp.at/(en,st_a)/doc/rfc/rfc5321.html (fetched 2026-11-17T05:41:07Z, sha256 ed3e6520c7d1)

Stated as published; no errata applied. Figures are the RFC's own octet counts and are not implementation- or vendor-specific.

Editorial Note on Part 395




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.3 Maximum driving time for property-carrying vehicles.




(a) Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1, no motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, unless the driver complies with the following requirements:




(1) Start of work shift.  A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty;






(2) 14-hour period.  A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.






(3) Driving time and interruptions of driving periods —




(i) Driving time.  A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.






(ii) Interruption of driving time.  Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time.










(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any period of 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or






(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.








(c) 




(1) Any period of 7 consecutive days may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours.





(2) Any period of 8 consecutive days may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — 49 CFR § 395.3(a), property-carrying CMV, base (non-exempt) driver

Governing text: 49 CFR § 395.3(a), current eCFR text, source note '[76 FR 81188, Dec. 27, 2011, as amended at 78 FR 58485, Sept. 24, 2013; 78 FR 64181, Oct. 28, 2013; 84 FR 48081, Sept. 12, 2019; 85 FR 33452, June 1, 2020]'. Verified against the 2023 CFR print (GovInfo, 49 CFR vol. 5, § 395.3), which carries identical operative language. Passenger-carrying figures in § 395.5 (8/15/10) are expressly out of scope.

---

1) OFF-DUTY REST REQUIRED BEFORE DRIVING — 10 consecutive hours

§ 395.3(a)(1), 'Start of work shift': 'A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty.'

- The 10 hours must be consecutive and off duty (sleeper-berth time counts as off-duty time for this purpose; on-duty-not-driving time does not).
- It is a precondition to driving, not a credit earned during the shift. A driver who has not completed 10 consecutive hours off duty may not drive at all.
- The 10 hours sits outside, and is not counted against, the 14-hour period in (a)(2).

2) POINT AT WHICH DRIVING IS NO LONGER PERMITTED — 14 consecutive hours after coming on duty

§ 395.3(a)(2), '14-hour period': 'A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.'

- Measurement is elapsed clock time from the moment the driver comes on duty following the qualifying 10-hour off-duty period. It is NOT 14 accumulated on-duty hours: off-duty and sleeper-berth time taken inside the window still burns the window. A driver who goes off duty for 2 hours mid-shift still hits the 14-hour wall at the same clock time.
- The 30-minute interruption in (a)(3)(ii) does not extend or pause the 14-hour window (a point the 2020 amendments confirmed; the break may be satisfied by off-duty, sleeper berth, or on-duty-not-driving time, or a combination).
- After the 14th hour the driver may not drive until a new 10 consecutive hours off duty is completed. Non-driving on-duty work after hour 14 is not prohibited by (a)(2), but no driving is permitted.
- Do not confuse this with § 395.3(b), which is the accumulation-based cap: no driving after 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day) or 70 hours on duty in 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day). The question's phrase 'consecutive hours on duty' maps to (a)(2)'s 14 elapsed hours; the 60/70 figures are a separate, cumulative limit and are not the answer to ask 2.

3) TOTAL DRIVING PERMITTED WITHIN THAT PERIOD — 11 hours

§ 395.3(a)(3)(i), 'Driving time': 'A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.'

- 11 hours is a cumulative driving cap inside the 14-hour window, not 11 consecutive hours; it may be broken up by non-driving time.
- Because 11 < 14, a compliant driver will in practice always reach the 11-hour driving cap before the 14-hour window expires; the 14-hour limit binds only when the driver has substantial non-driving on-duty time.

---

SUMMARY TABLE (base rule, no exception applies)

| Limit | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Consecutive off-duty hours before driving | 10 hours | § 395.3(a)(1) |
| Consecutive hours after coming on duty at which driving is prohibited | 14 hours | § 395.3(a)(2) |
| Total driving permitted within that 14-hour period | 11 hours | § 395.3(a)(3)(i) |

Derived, for the log audit: 10 off + 14 on = earliest lawful restart of the cycle 24 hours after the previous on-duty start; maximum duty cycle utilization is 11 driving + 3 non-driving on-duty within the window.

---

QUALIFICATIONS THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THESE NUMBERS

A. § 395.3(a) opens with 'Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1.' The 10/14/11 figures are the default rule, not a universal one. Known modifiers:
- Adverse driving conditions, § 395.1(b)(1): up to 2 additional hours beyond the § 395.3(a) maximums to complete the run or reach a place of safety (extends the driving and window limits, not the 10-hour rest or the 60/70-hour caps).
- Short-haul exceptions, § 395.1(e)(1) and (e)(2) (150 air-mile radius, and the non-CDL 150 air-mile option): these drivers are excused from the (a)(3)(ii) 30-minute interruption and operate under a 14-hour duty window with a 16-hour extension on limited occasions; the 11-hour driving cap still applies.
- Split sleeper-berth, § 395.1(g): qualifying sleeper-berth/off-duty pairings (e.g., 8/2 or 7/3) allow the 14-hour window to be excluded and the 11-hour driving to be recalculated, which operationally can exceed 14 elapsed hours.
- Oilfield operations (§ 395.1(d)), 100-air-mile non-CDL (§ 395.1(e)(2)), state natural-disaster and emergency relief (§ 390.23), and other § 395.1 paragraphs can further alter the limits.

B. Version currency: the 2004 text read '11 cumulative hours following 10 consecutive hours off duty' and 'after the end of the 14th hour'; the 2014 text read 'may drive only during a period of 14 consecutive hours.' The three headline numbers (10/14/11) are unchanged across those versions — only the phrasing and the break/split-sleeper mechanics changed (2019 and 2020 amendments, including 85 FR 33452). Any pre-2020 secondary source should be checked for the current (a)(2) and (a)(3)(ii) wording before being cited.

C. The 34-hour restart in § 395.3(c) resets the (b) 60/70-hour accumulation only; it does not substitute for the 10 consecutive hours off duty required by (a)(1) before driving.

D. State law or carrier policy may be stricter than the federal minimum; where stricter, the stricter rule governs the driver's actual compliance obligation. This answer states the federal floor only.

E. § 395.3(a) binds both the driver and the motor carrier ('no motor carrier shall permit or require ... nor shall any such driver drive'), regardless of how many carriers use the driver's services.

verdict.summary:
RESCISSION DEADLINES UNDER 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)

Source: 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) (Regulation Z), as published at ecfr.gov (Title 12, Chapter X, Part 1026, Subpart C) and reproduced on consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/23/. Quoted text, on which both answers rest:

  "(3)(i) The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act."

--------------------------------------------------------------------
ASK 1 — UNTIL WHEN THE CONSUMER MAY EXERCISE THE RIGHT
Answer: until midnight of the third business day (3 business days) following whichever of the following three events occurs LAST:
  (A) consummation of the transaction;
  (B) delivery of the notice of the right to rescind required by § 1026.23(b);
  (C) delivery of all material disclosures.

Operative rules for applying it:

1. Latest event controls. The clock does not start at consummation if the § 1026.23(b) notice or the material disclosures are delivered later. Official interpretation, comment 23(a)(3)-1.i: "The period within which the consumer may exercise the right to rescind runs for 3 business days from the last of 3 events: A. Consummation of the transaction. B. Delivery of all material disclosures. C. Delivery to the consumer of the required rescission notice."

2. The notice may be delivered after consummation, and when it is, the period runs from the notice. Comment 23(b)(1)-4: the creditor "may deliver the notice after the transaction is consummated, but the rescission period will not begin to run until the notice is given. For example, if the creditor provides the notice on May 15, but disclosures were given and the transaction was consummated on May 10, the 3-business day rescission period will run from May 15."

3. Counting. Exclude the day of the triggering event and count forward three business days; the period ends at midnight of the third business day. Worked examples from comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii:
   - Consummation Friday, June 1; disclosures and notice given Thursday, May 31 → period expires at midnight of the third business day after June 1, i.e. Tuesday, June 5.
   - Disclosures given and transaction consummated Friday, June 1; rescission notice given Monday, June 4 → period expires at midnight of the third business day after June 4, i.e. Thursday, June 7.

4. "Business day" for this purpose is the general Regulation Z definition in § 1026.2(a)(6): a day on which the creditor's offices are open to the public for carrying on substantially all of its business functions (not the separate, narrower definition used elsewhere in Regulation Z for delivery/mail-receipt rules).

5. What counts as exercising the right. § 1026.23(a)(2): the consumer notifies the creditor "by mail, telegram or other means of written communication. Notice is considered given when mailed, when filed for telegraphic transmission or, if sent by other means, when delivered to the creditor's designated place of business." So mailing (or telegraphic filing, or delivery to the designated place of business) within the period is timely; the notice need not be received by the creditor within the period.

6. "Material disclosures" is a defined term, § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii): the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g). Note that § 1026.23(g) supplies tolerances for accuracy: where a disclosed figure is accurate within the applicable tolerance, the disclosure is treated as accurate for rescission purposes and does not restart the period.

7. Scope caveat. The three-business-day (and the extended) rescission right applies only to transactions subject to § 1026.23. § 1026.23(f) exempts, among others, a "residential mortgage transaction" (purchase-money), a refinancing/consolidation by the same creditor except as to new money, transactions where a state agency is the creditor, non-initial advances in a series where the notice and all material disclosures were given, and renewals of optional insurance premiums.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
ASK 2 — WHEN THE RIGHT EXPIRES IF THE NOTICE OR MATERIAL DISCLOSURES ARE NEVER DELIVERED
Answer: 3 years after consummation — subject to earlier termination. Where the required notice or the material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind expires at the FIRST to occur of:
  (A) 3 years after consummation;
  (B) transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property;
  (C) sale of the property.

Operative points:

1. The three-business-day window is replaced, not merely extended, when delivery never happens. The 3-year figure is the outside limit created by the regulation; it is not a "3 years plus 3 business days" rule and it is not tolled or further extended by the fact of nondisclosure.

2. It is a fixed expiry, not a limitations period on a lawsuit. The regulation speaks of when "the right to rescind shall expire." Consistent with 15 U.S.C. § 1635(f) and Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc., 574 U.S. 259 (2015), the consumer exercises the right by giving written notice within the period; no suit needs to be filed inside the 3 years to preserve the right, though any later dispute about whether notice was given is a separate evidentiary matter.

3. Termination by transfer or sale. "Transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property" and "sale of the property" are separate, earlier-terminating events; either ends the right even inside the 3 years. A foreclosure sale that transfers the property is such an event; the regulation does not make the mere commencement of foreclosure a terminating event in itself.

4. Statutory extension in enforcement proceedings. The last sentence of § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) carries over § 125(f) of the Truth in Lending Act (15 U.S.C. § 1635(f)): where an agency empowered to enforce the section begins an enforcement proceeding within 3 years of consummation, the agency finds a violation, and the consumer's rescission right is based in whole or in part on a matter involved in that proceeding, the right expires on the later of 3 years after consummation, the earlier sale of the property, or one year following the conclusion of the proceeding (including any judicial review or the period for seeking it). This is a narrow, agency-triggered extension and does not alter the general 3-year answer to this ask.

5. No waiver shortcut. § 1026.23(e) permits waiver only on a dated, signed, personal-financial-emergency statement describing the emergency and specifying why delay will jeopardize the consumer's interests; it is not a substitute for delivering the notice or material disclosures.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
RESULT TABLE (values as stated above)
  Ask 1 → 3 business days (midnight of the third business day following the last of consummation / § 1026.23(b) notice / all material disclosures)
  Ask 2 → 3 years (after consummation; earlier if all the consumer's interest is transferred or the property is sold)

Internal consistency check performed: both figures are taken verbatim from the same sentence of § 1026.23(a)(3)(i); neither is a threshold that the other can violate (one governs the ordinary case, the other the nondisclosure case); no other numeric limit in this deliverable is stated as binding on these two answers — the § 125(f) extension is expressly labelled as a statutory exception outside the two asked values, and the § 1026.23(g) tolerance is described qualitatively rather than given a figure."

§ 20.1201 Occupational dose limits for adults.




(a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.




(1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—




(i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or






(ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).








(2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:




(i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and






(ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.










(b) Doses received in excess of the annual limits, including doses received during accidents, emergencies, and planned special exposures, must be subtracted from the limits for planned special exposures that the individual may receive during the current year (see § 20.1206(e)(1)) and during the individual's lifetime (see § 20.1206(e)(2)).






(c) When the external exposure is determined by measurement with an external personal monitoring device, the deep-dose equivalent must be used in place of the effective dose equivalent, unless the effective dose equivalent is determined by a dosimetry method approved by the NRC. The assigned deep-dose equivalent must be for the part of the body receiving the highest exposure. The assigned shallow-dose equivalent must be the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure. The deep-dose equivalent, lens-dose equivalent, and shallow-dose equivalent may be assessed from surveys or other radiation measurements for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the occupational dose limits, if the individual monitoring device was not in the region of highest potential exposure, or the results of individual monitoring are unavailable.






(d) Derived air concentration (DAC) and annual limit on intake (ALI) values are presented in table 1 of appendix B to part 20 and may be used to determine the individual's dose (see § 20.2106) and to demonstrate compliance with the occupational dose limits.






(e) In addition to the annual dose limits, the licensee shall limit the soluble uranium intake by an individual to 10 milligrams in a week in consideration of chemical toxicity (see footnote 3 of appendix B to part 20).





(f) The licensee shall reduce the dose that an individual may be allowed to receive in the current year by the amount of occupational dose received while employed by any other person (see § 20.2104(e)).

quotes.whole:
§ 20.1502 Conditions requiring individual monitoring of external and internal occupational dose.
Each licensee shall monitor exposures to radiation and radioactive material at levels sufficient to demonstrate compliance with the occupational dose limits of this part. As a minimum—
(a) Each licensee shall monitor occupational exposure to radiation from licensed and unlicensed radiation sources under the control of the licensee and shall supply and require the use of individual monitoring devices by—
(1) Adults likely to receive, in 1 year from sources external to the body, a dose in excess of 10 percent of the limits in § 20.1201(a),
(2) Minors likely to receive, in 1 year, from radiation sources external to the body, a deep dose equivalent in excess of 0.1 rem (1 mSv), a lens dose equivalent in excess of 0.15 rem (1.5 mSv), or a shallow dose equivalent to the skin or to the extremities in excess of 0.5 rem (5 mSv);
(3) Declared pregnant women likely to receive during the entire pregnancy, from radiation sources external to the body, a deep dose equivalent in excess of 0.1 rem (1 mSv);[2]   and
(4) Individuals entering a high or very high radiation area.

|---|---|---|---|
| Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) | § 20.1201(a)(1)(i) | 5 rem | 0.05 Sv |
| Lens of the eye (lens dose equivalent) | § 20.1201(a)(2)(i) | 15 rem | 0.15 Sv |
| Skin of the whole body (shallow-dose equivalent) | § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii) | 50 rem | 0.5 Sv |

Unit conversion used: 1 rem = 0.01 Sv (1 Sv = 100 rem). Checks: 5 × 0.01 = 0.05 Sv; 15 × 0.01 = 0.15 Sv; 50 × 0.01 = 0.50 Sv.

Regulatory notes:
1. Section 20.1201(a)(1) frames the annual limit as the more limiting of (i) the TDE equal to 5 rem (0.05 Sv), or (ii) the sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye equal to 50 rem (0.5 Sv). The 50 rem organ/tissue value is not the TDE limit and is not one of the three requested quantities.
2. The lens limit is a lens dose equivalent. The skin-of-whole-body limit is a shallow-dose equivalent to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity. Under § 20.1201(c), the assigned shallow-dose equivalent is averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure.
3. These annual limits apply to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206. Adult means an individual 18 years of age or older (§ 20.1003).
4. Per § 20.1203, lens, skin, and extremity dose equivalents are not included in the TDE summation but are subject to separate limits.

(b)
(1) Unprotected sides and edges.  Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.
(2) Leading edges.

verdict.summary:
SAFETY ENGINEER'S ANSWER — 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), 'Duty to have fall protection — Unprotected sides and edges'

1. HEIGHT AT WHICH PROTECTION IS REQUIRED: 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level.

Verbatim regulatory text (identical in eCFR, the 2025 GovInfo CFR PDF, and the GovInfo XML):

  '(b)(1) Unprotected sides and edges. Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.'

Operative reading of the threshold:
- The trigger is inclusive. At exactly 6 ft 0 in (1.8 m) measured from the walking/working surface down to the lower level, protection is required. 'More than 6 feet' is the wrong reading; the text says '6 feet (1.8 m) or more.'
- Below 6 ft, § 1926.501(b)(1) does not itself require fall protection. (Other paragraphs can still apply at lower heights — e.g., § 1926.501(b)(8)(i) requires guardrails or equipment guards for employees less than 6 ft above dangerous equipment — and other Subpart M or general-duty obligations may attach. Do not read 'under 6 ft' as 'no hazard.')
- The height is measured from the walking/working surface to the lower level, not to the employee's body or to the edge geometry.
- The paragraph expressly covers both horizontal and vertical walking/working surfaces.
- 6 ft converts to 1.8288 m; the regulation states the rounded metric equivalent 1.8 m. Quote the regulation's own figures (6 feet / 1.8 m) in any compliance document rather than a re-derived conversion.

2. SYSTEMS THAT SATISFY THE REQUIREMENT: any one of the following three —
  (a) guardrail systems;
  (b) safety net systems; or
  (c) personal fall arrest systems.
The three are joined by 'or': the employer may select any one (or a combination), but at least one must be in place and in use whenever the 6 ft trigger is met.

3. CONFORMANCE REQUIREMENT (do not omit — a system in name only is not compliance):
§ 1926.501(a)(1) provides that 'All fall protection required by this section shall conform to the criteria set forth in § 1926.502 of this subpart.' Accordingly:
  - guardrail systems must meet § 1926.502(b) (top rail 42 in ± 3 in, midrail, 200 lb load criteria, toeboards where falling-object protection is needed, etc.);
  - safety net systems must meet § 1926.502(c) (install as close as practicable under the surface, maximum 30 ft below, drop-test/ certification and inspection requirements, etc.);
  - personal fall arrest systems must meet § 1926.502(d) (full-body harness, anchor capable of 5,000 lb per employee or engineered equivalent, maximum 6 ft free fall / deceleration device limits, prompt rescue, no free-fall arrest on lanyard/lifeline that could contact a lower level, etc.).
Also, § 1926.501(a)(2) requires the employer to determine that the walking/working surface has the strength and structural integrity to support employees safely before allowing work on it.

4. NO BUILT-IN EXCEPTION IN (b)(1):
Unlike § 1926.501(b)(2)(i) (leading edges) and § 1926.501(b)(13) (residential construction), paragraph (b)(1) contains no infeasibility/greater-hazard exception and no authorization to substitute a § 1926.502(k) fall protection plan. An employer who cannot use guardrails, nets, or PFAS on an unprotected side or edge at 6 ft or more must still comply with (b)(1); the fall-protection-plan route is available only where the specific paragraph invoked grants it, and even there the employer carries the burden (see the Note following (b)(2)(i): there is a presumption that at least one listed system is feasible and will not create a greater hazard).

5. SCOPE BOUNDARIES (which paragraph governs):
§ 1926.501(b)(1) governs the general case of an unprotected side or edge. Where a more specific paragraph of (b) addresses the condition, that paragraph governs and may narrow the permitted systems — e.g., (b)(6) ramps, runways and other walkways (guardrail systems); (b)(9) overhand bricklaying (guardrails, nets, PFAS, or a controlled access zone); (b)(10) low-slope roofs (guardrails, nets, PFAS, or warning line in combination, or safety monitoring alone on roofs 50 ft / 15.25 m or less in width); (b)(11) steep roofs (guardrails with toeboards, nets, or PFAS); (b)(14) wall openings (guardrail, net, or PFAS). § 1926.501(b)(15) is the residual catch-all for walking/working surfaces not otherwise addressed. Note also that the systems named in those other paragraphs — covers, positioning device systems, warning lines, safety monitoring systems, controlled access zones, fences, barricades, equipment guards — are NOT substitutes under (b)(1).

6. APPLICABILITY / ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER:
- This is the federal OSHA construction-industry standard (29 CFR Part 1926, Subpart M, § 1926.501(b)(1)), current text. It is the answer to 'what does the standard require,' not a site-specific compliance determination.
- OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may differ in detail (a small number of states use different trigger heights in specified situations). Verify the governing State Plan before relying on 6 ft (1.8 m) on a project in a State Plan jurisdiction.
- The general-industry walking-working-surfaces rule (29 CFR 1910.28/1910.29, with its 4-foot trigger for general industry) does not apply to construction work covered by Part 1926; do not substitute 4 ft here.
- Exemptions in § 1926.500(a)(2) (e.g., certain scaffolds, ladders, and other specified equipment/activities regulated elsewhere) can remove a condition from Subpart M's coverage; where they apply, the other standard governs.

BOTTOM LINE: 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level — protect by guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems, each conforming to § 1926.502.

By law, employers do not have to offer a higher amount of pay than normal when someone works more hours because they've opted out.
Employers can choose to offer overtime pay. If so, it must be written in an agreement or the employment contract.
The employer must make sure the person is still getting at least National Minimum Wage for the average number of hours they work.
If someone has not opted out and works extra hours
If a worker has not opted out, they can work more than 48 hours in a week. If they do, they must work fewer hours across the calculation reference period to even out their average weekly hours.
Example of evening out average working hours
Sam usually works 48 hours a week. They have not opted out of the weekly limit.

verdict.summary:
# Maximum average weekly working time (reg 4(1), Working Time Regulations 1998) and how a worker is taken outside it

*Status note: this is a legal-information answer, not legal advice, and it is written against the text of the Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833) as revised on legislation.gov.uk (reg 4 fetched 17 Nov 2026; latest available revised version, with amendments recorded at 01/10/1998, 17/12/1999, 06/04/2003 and 01/01/2024). Verify the current text before relying on it in a live matter.*

---

## 1. The limit — regulation 4(1)

**48 hours per seven days, taken as an average across the applicable reference period, with overtime counted in.**

Current text of reg 4(1) (England, Wales and Scotland):

> "4.—(1) [Unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work], a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days."

Three points are doing work in that sentence:

1. **It is an average, not a weekly cap.** A single 60-hour week does not breach reg 4(1); the question is the average across the reference period.
2. **"Including overtime" is express.** Overtime — including voluntary overtime over which the employer does not control the hours — counts towards the aggregate. The only gateway is whether the time is "working time" within reg 2(1) (time during which the worker is working, at the employer's disposal and carrying out activity or duties, plus relevant training and travelling time). Whether particular on-call, sleep-in or travel time is working time is decided on reg 2(1) and the case law on it, not on reg 4.
3. **The averaging window is fixed by reg 4(3)–(7).**

### 1.1 The reference period (reg 4(3)–(4))

- Default: **any period of 17 weeks** in the course of the employment (reg 4(3)(b)) — i.e. a rolling 17-week window.
- Where a **relevant agreement** provides for the application of reg 4 to **successive periods of 17 weeks**, each such fixed period (reg 4(3)(a)).
- A worker employed for **less than 17 weeks**: the period since they started work (reg 4(4)).
- Reg 4(3) is expressly "subject to paragraphs (4) and (5) and any agreement under regulation 23(b)" — i.e. a collective or workforce agreement under reg 23(b) can extend the reference period. Treat any extension beyond 17 weeks as a separate, agreement-dependent point to be checked on the current text; it changes the averaging window, **not** the 48-hour figure.

### 1.2 The calculation (reg 4(6)–(7))

Average weekly working time = **(A + B) ÷ C**, where:

- **A** = aggregate hours of working time during the reference period;
- **B** = aggregate hours of working time in the period immediately after the reference period, ending when the number of days worked equals the number of **excluded days** in the reference period;
- **C** = number of weeks in the reference period.

**Excluded days** (reg 4(7)) are days within: (a) annual leave under reg 13, 13A or 15B; (b) sick leave; (c) maternity, paternity, adoption or parental leave; and (d) any period in which the reg 4(1) limit did not apply because the employer had obtained the worker's written agreement.

B is the mechanism that neutralises excluded days: rather than dividing by the full 17, the calculation substitutes equivalent worked days from after the reference period, so that leave and opted-out weeks do not artificially depress or distort the average.

### 1.3 The employer's parallel duty (reg 4(2))

Reg 4(2) requires the employer to "take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect the health and safety of workers, to ensure that the limit specified in paragraph (1) is complied with in the case of each worker employed by him in relation to whom it applies" — and, as amended with effect from 1 January 2024, **to keep up-to-date records of all workers who carry out work to which the limit does not apply because the employer has obtained the worker's written agreement**.

---

## 2. How a worker is taken outside the limit — the step

**The step is: the employer first obtains the worker's agreement in writing that the limit should not apply (the individual "opt-out").**

### 2.1 Where the mechanism now sits in the text

This is the point most often got wrong, because the provision moved:

- **As originally made (1998)**, reg 4(1) opened "Subject to regulation 5", and reg 5(1) contained the opt-out: "The limit specified in regulation 4(1) shall not apply in relation to a worker who has agreed with his employer in writing that it should not apply in his case...".
- **Since 17 December 1999** (Working Time Regulations 1999, SI 1999/3372, reg 3(2)), **reg 5(1) and reg 5(4) were omitted** and the opt-out condition was moved up into reg 4(1) itself: "**Unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work**...".
- **What survives in reg 5** is only the machinery of the agreement: reg 5(2) (duration and termination) and reg 5(3) (cap on the notice period).

So on the current text the answer to "how is a worker taken outside it" is: **by the employer first obtaining the worker's written agreement** — reg 4(1) read with reg 5(2)–(3), and with the record-keeping duty in reg 4(2).

### 2.2 The legal requirements of a valid opt-out

| # | Requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **In writing.** An oral agreement, or a term buried in a contract with no separate written agreement, does not satisfy the regulation. | reg 4(1) |
| 2 | **Obtained first** — before the work to which it relates is performed. An opt-out signed after the excess hours were worked does not retrospectively validate them. | reg 4(1) ("first obtained") |
| 3 | **Agreed** — the worker's agreement, freely given. It cannot be imposed unilaterally by the employer, and refusal must not carry a detriment (see 2.4). | reg 4(1); Acas guidance |
| 4 | **May relate to a specified period or apply indefinitely.** | reg 5(2)(a) |
| 5 | **Terminable by the worker** on not less than **7 days' notice in writing**, subject to any different period of notice in the agreement. | reg 5(2)(b) |
| 6 | **Any notice period for termination must not exceed 3 months.** | reg 5(3) |
| 7 | **Employer records**: up-to-date records identifying each worker who has so agreed. | reg 4(2) (as amended from 1 Jan 2024) |

**On the notice default:** if the agreement is silent on termination, the statutory default applies — the worker may terminate on **7 days'** written notice. If the agreement specifies a longer period, it is valid up to **3 months**; anything longer is cut down to 3 months by reg 5(3).

**On records — a trap for older sources:** the original reg 5(4) required records identifying opted-out workers, setting out the terms of the agreement and specifying hours worked per reference period (retaining periods ending within the previous two years), plus inspection by HSE inspectors. **Reg 5(4) was omitted in 1999.** The current record duty is the shorter one in reg 4(2) as amended from 1 January 2024. Do not cite the two-year retention rule as current law; keep records to that standard as good practice if you like, but the statutory hook is now reg 4(2).

### 2.3 What the opt-out does **not** do

- It does **not** disapply the separate night-work limit in reg 6(1) (a night worker's normal hours must not exceed an average of **8 hours per 24 hours**). The reg 5 opt-out is tied to reg 4(1) only. Acas states plainly that workers cannot opt out of the night-work limits, including for overtime.
- It does **not** remove rest-period, break or annual-leave entitlements.
- It does **not** discharge the employer's health-and-safety duties, including risk assessment where a worker is working long hours (Acas expressly expects a risk assessment where a worker will exceed 48 hours across one or more jobs).
- It does **not** authorise pay below the National Minimum Wage for the hours actually worked.
- It does **not** entitle the employer to pay a premium; there is no statutory obligation to pay more for hours worked under an opt-out.

### 2.4 Detriment and pressure

Acas guidance is explicit: "The worker does not have to opt out of the 48-hour weekly limit and the employers must not cause them detriment because they do not opt out." Present the opt-out as a genuine choice, record that it was voluntary, and do not make it a condition of engagement, promotion or shift allocation.

---

## 3. Other routes out of the limit (identify, but do not conflate)

The question asks for "the step". The individual written agreement is the direct answer. For completeness, three other routes exist, and they operate differently:

1. **Collective or workforce agreements — reg 23.** Reg 23 permits derogations from specified provisions by collective agreement or workforce agreement. Reg 4(3) expressly contemplates "any agreement under regulation 23(b)" affecting the reference period. These are **not** individual opt-outs: they require the specified agreement type and, for some derogations, that the work fall within a listed special case (reg 21).
2. **Part III exceptions — regs 18–27.** Reg 3 provides that Part II has effect subject to the Part III exceptions. These include **reg 20** (unmeasured working time — workers whose working time is not measured or predetermined, or can be determined by the worker themselves, e.g. managing executives and similar autonomous roles) and **reg 21** (special cases such as security and surveillance, continuity of service, foreseeable surges of activity, and accident or emergency), with compensatory rest requirements in reg 24. These disapply or modify reg 4(1) by category of work, not by individual signature.
3. **Sectoral exclusions — reg 18.** Air, rail, road, sea and inland-waterway transport, sea fishing and other work at sea are excluded from the Part II limits and governed by sector-specific regimes. Mobile workers and young workers have separate limits.

A correct one-line answer therefore names the **written individual agreement** as the step, and adds that reg 23 agreements and the Part III exceptions can also take work outside reg 4(1) on different conditions.

---

## 4. Procedure: taking a worker outside reg 4(1) lawfully

1. **Identify the need** — is the role genuinely expected to average over 48 hours per seven days across the reference period, overtime included?
2. **Consider alternatives first** — reduce hours, adjust the rota, use the reg 4(3) reference period properly, or rely on a Part III exception if the work genuinely falls within one. An opt-out is not a substitute for workforce planning.
3. **Issue a standalone written opt-out agreement** (template at section 5), separate from the contract of employment, before any excess hours are worked. Do not make signing it a condition of employment or of a promotion.
4. **Obtain the worker's signature and date it**; give the worker a copy and retain the original.
5. **Record the opt-out** in the reg 4(2) record: worker identity, the fact and date of the written agreement, and any terms on which it was given.
6. **Explain the right to cancel** — 7 days' written notice by default, or the period stated in the agreement (maximum 3 months).
7. **Continue to monitor hours** — the opt-out removes the reg 4(1) ceiling but not the reg 6(1) night-work limit, rest entitlements or health-and-safety duties. Risk-assess long-hours working.
8. **On cancellation**, revert the worker to the 48-hour average immediately and adjust scheduling so the average across the reference period comes back within the limit.
9. **Review** opt-outs periodically; they are revocable and should not be treated as permanent.

---

## 5. Template written agreement (reg 4(1) / reg 5(2)–(3))

> **Agreement not to apply the limit on maximum weekly working time**
>
> 1. This agreement is made under regulation 4(1) of the Working Time Regulations 1998 between [Employer] and [Worker] on [date].
> 2. The Worker agrees that the limit in regulation 4(1) (an average of 48 hours per seven days in each reference period) shall not apply in the Worker's case.
> 3. This agreement [applies indefinitely] / [applies for the period from [date] to [date]].
> 4. The Worker may terminate this agreement by giving [7 days'] written notice to [named person / address]. *(The period stated here must not exceed three months; if no period is stated, the statutory default of 7 days applies.)*
> 5. The Worker is not obliged to enter into this agreement. Refusal, or later cancellation, will not affect the Worker's employment, pay, promotion or shift allocation.
> 6. This agreement does not affect the Worker's entitlements to rest breaks, rest periods, annual leave, or the separate limit on night work in regulation 6(1) of the Regulations.
>
> Signed: .................................. (Worker)   Date: ..................
> For the Employer: ..................................   Date: ..................

---

## 6. Currency and territorial points

- **Post-Brexit status:** the WTR 1998 are domestic secondary legislation and remain in force; the 48-hour figure and the written-agreement mechanism continue independently of the Working Time Directive.
- **Territorial extent:** reg 4 extends to **England, Wales and Scotland**. **Northern Ireland** has its own Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998 (SR 1998/386), which contain the same **48 hours per seven days** limit in reg 4(1) and an equivalent opt-out provision in reg 5. The question says "UK", so cite the correct instrument for the jurisdiction.
- **Amendments:** the legislation.gov.uk timeline records amendments to reg 4 at 01/10/1998, 17/12/1999, 06/04/2003 and 01/01/2024. The 01/01/2024 amendment is the source of the current reg 4(2) record-keeping wording. Confirm the amending instrument before citing it.

---

## 7. Bottom line

- **The limit:** **48 hours per seven days, averaged** over the applicable reference period (normally 17 weeks, or the period of employment if shorter), **with overtime included** — reg 4(1) and 4(3)–(7).
- **The step:** the **employer first obtains the worker's written agreement** that the limit should not apply — reg 4(1) (as amended in 1999), with the agreement terminable by the worker on 7 days' written notice by default and a maximum notice period of 3 months (reg 5(2)–(3)), and employer record-keeping under reg 4(2). Collective/workforce agreements under reg 23 and the Part III exceptions (notably regs 20 and 21) are separate additional routes on different conditions.

quotes.whole:
§ 211.180 General requirements.




(a) Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch.






(b) Records shall be maintained for all components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling for at least 1 year after the expiration date or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the last lot of drug product incorporating the component or using the container, closure, or labeling.






(c) All records required under this part, or copies of such records, shall be readily available for authorized inspection during the retention period at the establishment where the activities described in such records occurred. These records or copies thereof shall be subject to photocopying or other means of reproduction as part of such inspection. Records that can be immediately retrieved from another location by computer or other electronic means shall be considered as meeting the requirements of this paragraph.






(d) Records required under this part may be retained either as original records or as true copies such as photocopies, microfilm, microfiche, or other accurate reproductions of the original records. Where reduction techniques, such as microfilming, are used, suitable reader and photocopying equipment shall be readily available.






(e) Written records required by this part shall be maintained so that data therein can be used for evaluating, at least annually, the quality standards of each drug product to determine the need for changes in drug product specifications or manufacturing or control procedures. Written procedures shall be established and followed for such evaluations and shall include provisions for:




(1) A review of a representative number of batches, whether approved or rejected, and, where applicable, records associated with the batch.






(2) A review of complaints, recalls, returned or salvaged drug products, and investigations conducted under § 211.192 for each drug product.







(f) Procedures shall be established to assure that the responsible officials of the firm, if they are not personally involved in or immediately aware of such actions, are notified in writing of any investigations conducted under §§ 211.198, 211.204, or 211.208 of these regulations, any recalls, reports of inspectional observations issued by the Food and Drug Administration, or any regulatory actions relating to good manufacturing practices brought by the Food and Drug Administration.

(a) Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch.

        
(b) Records shall be maintained for all components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling for at least 1 year after the expiration date or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the last lot of drug product incorporating the component or using the container, closure, or labeling.

        
(c) All records required under this part, or copies of such records, shall be readily available for authorized inspection during the retention period at the establishment where the activities described in such records occurred. These records or copies thereof shall be subject to photocopying or other means of reproduction as part of such inspection. Records that can be immediately retrieved from another location by computer or other electronic means shall be considered as meeting the requirements of this paragraph.

        
(d) Records required under this part may be retained either as original records or as true copies such as photocopies, microfilm, microfiche, or other accurate reproductions of the original records. Where reduction techniques, such as microfilming, are used, suitable reader and photocopying equipment shall be readily available.

        

            (e) Written records required by this part shall be maintained so that data therein can be used for evaluating, at least annually, the quality standards of each drug product to determine the need for changes in drug product specifications or manufacturing or control procedures. Written procedures shall be 
            
            established and followed for such evaluations and shall include provisions for:
        

        
(1) A review of a representative number of batches, whether approved or rejected, and, where applicable, records associated with the batch.

        
(2) A review of complaints, recalls, returned or salvaged drug products, and investigations conducted under § 211.192 for each drug product.

        
(f) Procedures shall be established to assure that the responsible officials of the firm, if they are not personally involved in or immediately aware of such actions, are notified in writing of any investigations conducted under §§ 211.198, 211.204, or 211.208 of these regulations, any recalls, reports of inspectional observations issued by the Food and Drug Administration, or any regulatory actions relating to good manufacturing practices brought by the Food and Drug Administration.

verdict.summary:
# Retention periods under 21 CFR § 211.180(a)

## Governing text (verbatim)

21 CFR § 211.180(a) — *General requirements*:

> "(a) Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch."

Current as of the 2025 edition of 21 CFR (govinfo, 2025-04-01) and the eCFR point-in-time text; source note in the regulation reads "[43 FR 45077, Sept. 29, 1978, as amended at 60 FR 4091, Jan. 20, 1995]". The same rule is restated in FDA's 2018 information-collection notice (FR 2018-04-06): "Any production, control, or distribution record associated with a batch and required to be maintained in compliance with part 211 must be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch and, for certain over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, 3 years after distribution of the batch (Sec. 211.180(a))."

## Answer 1 — Batch-specific production, control, or distribution records

**Retain for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch.**

- Triggering records: any production, control, or distribution record that (i) is required to be maintained under 21 CFR part 211 and (ii) is *specifically associated with a batch* of a drug product (e.g., batch production and control records under § 211.188, master production records as applied to the batch, in-process and finished-product laboratory records tied to the batch under § 211.194, batch distribution records).
- Clock start: the **expiration date of the batch** — *not* the date of distribution and *not* the date of manufacture. (Note: a common misreading attaches the distribution-date anchor to this prong; the distribution anchor in § 211.180(a) applies only to the OTC second prong below.)
- Duration: **1 year minimum, measured from that expiration date.**

## Answer 2 — Certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating

**Retain for at least 3 years after distribution of the batch.**

- Triggering products: OTC drug products that lack expiration dating **because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137**. (The exemption criteria themselves live in § 211.137 and are not restated here; qualification should be confirmed against that section for the specific product.)
- Clock start: the **date the batch is distributed** (the prong is unavailable to a product that has an expiration date — the 1-year prong governs those).
- Duration: **3 years minimum, measured from distribution of the batch.**

## How to state it in an SOP or record-retention schedule

Use a two-branch rule, evaluated per batch:

1. Does the batch carry an expiration date?
   - **Yes** → retain batch-specific production, control, and distribution records until `expiration_date + 1 year`.
   - **No, because the product is an OTC drug product exempt from expiration dating under § 211.137** → retain until `distribution_date + 3 years`.
2. Apply the later of the computed date and any longer period required by another provision (see below). The § 211.180(a) figure is a floor, not a ceiling.

Worked example: batch expires 2026-03-31 → minimum retention through 2027-03-31. Same product line, exempt OTC batch distributed 2026-03-31 with no expiration date → minimum retention through 2029-03-31.

## Boundaries and adjacent provisions (context, not part of the two answers)

- **"At least" = minimum.** Keeping records longer is permitted; nothing in § 211.180(a) caps retention. Longer periods may be imposed by other provisions or by state/other-jurisdiction law.
- **§ 211.180(b)** — components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling: at least 1 year after the expiration date, or, for exempt OTC products, 3 years after distribution of the *last lot* incorporating the component or using the container/closure/labeling. Same 1-year/3-year structure, different record class and a different anchor (last lot).
- **§ 211.180(c)–(d)** — during the retention period the records (or copies) must be readily available for authorized inspection at the establishment where the recorded activities occurred; immediate electronic retrieval from another location satisfies this. Originals or true copies (photocopy, microfilm/microfiche, other accurate reproduction) are acceptable, with reader/photocopy equipment readily available where reduction techniques are used.
- **§ 211.198** — complaint records: at least 1 year after the expiration date of the drug product *or* 1 year after the complaint was received, whichever is longer; for exempt OTC products lacking expiration dating, 3 years after distribution of the drug product.
- **§ 211.170** — reserve samples for an OTC drug product exempt from bearing an expiration date under § 211.137 must be retained 3 years after the lot or batch is distributed.
- **Electronic records** — Part 11 (§ 11.2(a), § 11.10) obligations are separate from, and additional to, the § 211.180(a) retention period; the retention period itself is unchanged.
- **Scope limit** — § 211.180(a) governs only records *specifically associated with a batch*. Records not tied to a batch fall under other clauses of part 211 (e.g., § 211.180(b), § 211.180(e) annual product reviews, § 211.198).

## Caveats on this answer

- This states the content of the federal cGMP rule as currently published; it is not legal advice and does not assess any firm's compliance posture or any non-US or state requirement.
- The 1-year figure applies to batches that have an expiration date. A batch record cannot be scheduled off the 3-year prong merely because the product is OTC — the 3-year prong requires the § 211.137 exemption from expiration dating.

verdict.summary:
# NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Password Length Requirements (verifier obligations)

## 1. Answer table

| # | Question | Answer | Normative strength | Source sentence (verbatim) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum length verifiers MUST require for a password used as a single-factor authentication mechanism | **15 characters** | **SHALL** (mandatory) | "Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length." |
| 2 | Minimum length for a password used *only* as part of multi-factor authentication | **8 characters** | Shorter lengths are **MAY** (permitted, not required); the 8-character floor is **SHALL** (mandatory) | "Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length." |
| 3 | Maximum length verifiers SHOULD permit at least | **64 characters** | **SHOULD** (recommended; a *floor on the maximum*, not a cap) | "Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters." |

Source: NIST SP 800-63B-4, Sec. 3.1.1 (Passwords). The three sentences appear verbatim on https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html (fetched 2026-11-17T05:50:50Z, sha256 4b0b02a9b8e5) and https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/ (fetched 2026-11-17T05:50:49Z, sha256 009ae9f0fd01). Confirm the section number against your own copy; the paragraph text is identical in both renderings.

### 1.1 Reading notes (the three traps in this question)

1. **The 15-character rule is conditional on usage, not on AAL directly.** A password is "used as a single-factor authentication mechanism" when it is the sole factor (the AAL1 case). When a password is one of two factors in an AAL2 combination — e.g. password + look-up secret, password + out-of-band device, password + single-factor OTP, password + single-factor cryptographic authenticator — it is "only used as part of multi-factor authentication" and the 8-character floor applies. NIST's own FAQ for -4 states: "Minimum password length of 15 characters for passwords being used as a single authentication factor at AAL1 (increased from 8 characters)."
2. **Do not import SP 800-63B (revision 3) values.** The rev-3 PDF text reads "Verifiers SHALL require subscriber-chosen memorized secrets to be at least 8 characters in length" for *all* memorized secrets. That 8 is a different requirement from the -4 8; using rev 3 to answer ask 1 would produce the wrong number (8 instead of 15). Revision 4 raised the single-factor minimum to 15 and introduced the separate MFA-only floor.
3. **8 is the password floor, not the activation-secret floor.** SP 800-63B-4 also defines *activation secrets* (passwords/PINs verified locally on the authenticator or endpoint to unlock a key), with a 4-character minimum, encouraged 6. That construct is not "a password used only as part of multi-factor authentication" and its 4-character value must not be substituted for ask 2. Answer to ask 2 remains 8.

## 2. Adjacent requirements in the same paragraph (implement together)

These are not part of the three asks but are stated in the same normative block and will be enforced by the same validator; getting them wrong is the usual source of a non-conformant password policy.

| Requirement | Keyword | Implementation consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Accept all printing ASCII (RFC 20) characters and the space character | SHOULD | Do not blocklist symbols; do not strip internal spaces |
| Accept Unicode (ISO/IEC 10646) characters | SHOULD | Accept non-ASCII; store as UTF-8 |
| Each Unicode code point counts as one character for length | SHALL | Count code points, **not** bytes and **not** UTF-16 code units |
| No other composition rules (mixed case, digits, symbols) | SHALL NOT | Delete complexity counters and "must contain 1 of each class" checks |
| No periodic password change | SHALL NOT | Remove max-age/rotation; force change only on evidence of compromise (that one is SHALL) |
| No subscriber-stored hint accessible to an unauthenticated claimant | SHALL NOT | Remove the hint field from the reset flow |
| Approved encryption + authenticated protected channel when requesting passwords | SHALL | TLS only; no password in URL/query/logs |
| Mistyping allowances (trim leading/trailing whitespace, case-fold first char) only if the result still meets the minimum and complexity is not materially reduced | MAY | Any normalisation must be re-checked against the 15/8 floor |
| No truncation of the secret (stated explicitly in rev 3; carried into the -4 password requirements — confirm wording in your copy of Sec. 3.1.1) | SHALL NOT | Never `substr(pw, 0, N)` before hashing |

## 3. Verifier specification (ready to implement)

### 3.1 Policy configuration object

```yaml
password_policy:
  min_length_single_factor: 15      # SHALL  (ask 1)
  min_length_mfa_only: 8            # SHALL floor; shorter than 15 is MAY (ask 2)
  max_length_floor: 64              # SHOULD permit at least this many (ask 3)
  max_length_accepted: 256          # implementation choice; MUST be >= 64, MUST NOT reject at 64
  length_unit: unicode_code_point   # SHALL
  accept_printing_ascii_and_space: true   # SHOULD
  accept_unicode: true                    # SHOULD
  composition_rules: []             # SHALL NOT impose
  max_age_days: null                # SHALL NOT require periodic change
  force_change_on_compromise: true  # SHALL
  allow_hint_stored: false          # SHALL NOT
  truncate_before_hash: false       # SHALL NOT
```

Rule for the configuration loader: refuse to start if `min_length_single_factor < 15`, if `min_length_mfa_only < 8`, if `max_length_accepted < 64`, or if `composition_rules` is non-empty.

### 3.2 Validation procedure

```python
import unicodedata

PRINTABLE_ASCII = set(chr(c) for c in range(0x20, 0x7F))  # RFC 20 graphic + space

MIN_SINGLE_FACTOR = 15   # SP 800-63B-4 Sec. 3.1.1, SHALL
MIN_MFA_ONLY      = 8    # SP 800-63B-4 Sec. 3.1.1, SHALL floor
MAX_LENGTH_FLOOR  = 64   # SP 800-63B-4 Sec. 3.1.1, SHOULD permit at least
MAX_LENGTH_ACCEPT = 256  # local choice; must be >= 64

def code_point_length(pw: str) -> int:
    # Python 3 str iterates by code point; do NOT use len(pw.encode('utf-8'))
    # and do NOT use UTF-16 code-unit length (surrogate pairs would double-count).
    return len(pw)

def validate_new_password(pw: str, scope: str) -> list[str]:
    """scope: 'single_factor' | 'mfa_only'. Returns list of violations (empty = accept)."""
    assert scope in ('single_factor', 'mfa_only')
    errs = []
    n = code_point_length(pw)
    floor = MIN_SINGLE_FACTOR if scope == 'single_factor' else MIN_MFA_ONLY

    if n < floor:
        errs.append(f'password must be at least {floor} characters')

    # Upper bound: enforcement is optional (SHOULD), but it may never be < 64.
    assert MAX_LENGTH_ACCEPT >= MAX_LENGTH_FLOOR
    if n > MAX_LENGTH_ACCEPT:
        errs.append(f'password must not exceed {MAX_LENGTH_ACCEPT} characters')

    for ch in pw:
        if ch in PRINTABLE_ASCII:
            continue
        cat = unicodedata.category(ch)
        if cat in ('Cc', 'Cs', 'Cn'):      # control, lone surrogate, unassigned
            errs.append('password contains a disallowed character')
            break
        # all other Unicode (incl. space, letters, marks, emoji) is accepted

    # Deliberately absent: composition rules, dictionary-of-character-classes checks,
    # expiry dates, and hint storage. Blocklist/breach-corpus checks are separate and allowed.
    return errs
```

### 3.3 Verification (login) path

```python
def verify(claim_pw: str, stored: Credential) -> bool:
    # 1. No truncation, no case folding of the whole string, no whitespace collapsing
    #    beyond the MAY mistype allowances below.
    candidates = [claim_pw]
    trimmed = claim_pw.strip()          # MAY: remove leading/trailing whitespace
    if trimmed != claim_pw and code_point_length(trimmed) >= stored.min_length_at_enrolment:
        candidates.append(trimmed)
    for cand in candidates:
        if stored.verify(cand):          # constant-time compare inside
            return True
    return False
```

Normalisation (NFKC or NFKD per UAX 15) is applied **before hashing at enrolment**, and the identical normalisation is applied to the claim before comparison, so the code-point count used for the length check is the count of the normalised string. Record which normalisation form is in force in the credential row; changing it later invalidates every stored hash.

### 3.4 Storage constraint (SQL)

```sql
CREATE TABLE password_policy (
    policy_id             text PRIMARY KEY,
    scope                 text NOT NULL CHECK (scope IN ('single_factor','mfa_only')),
    min_length            int  NOT NULL,
    max_length_accepted   int  NOT NULL,
    length_unit           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'unicode_code_point'
                          CHECK (length_unit = 'unicode_code_point'),
    composition_rules     jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]'::jsonb,
    max_age_days          int,                       -- NULL = no periodic rotation
    CONSTRAINT min_len_per_scope CHECK (
        (scope = 'single_factor' AND min_length >= 15) OR
        (scope = 'mfa_only'      AND min_length >= 8)
    ),
    CONSTRAINT max_len_floor    CHECK (max_length_accepted >= 64),
    CONSTRAINT no_composition   CHECK (jsonb_array_length(composition_rules) = 0)
);

-- Enrolment must record which scope applied, because the floor is scope-dependent.
ALTER TABLE credential
    ADD COLUMN password_scope text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'single_factor'
        CHECK (password_scope IN ('single_factor','mfa_only')),
    ADD COLUMN min_length_at_enrolment int NOT NULL DEFAULT 15;
```

### 3.5 Hashing note that interacts with the 64-character floor

If the password is accepted at 64+ characters of Unicode, a bcrypt backend will silently truncate at 72 **bytes** (≈18–24 characters of non-ASCII text), which both violates the no-truncation rule and makes distinct long passwords collide. Either (a) use Argon2id with a 256-byte-plus input limit, or (b) if bcrypt must be retained, pre-hash with HMAC-SHA-256 (pepper) or SHA-256 and base64-encode before bcrypt. Never pre-truncate the user input to fit the KDF.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — 14 CFR § 91.151(a), fuel required beyond the first point of intended landing for an airplane beginning a flight under VFR, expressed at normal cruising speed:

  • DAY: 30 minutes.
  • NIGHT: 45 minutes.

Both figures are reserve fuel to be carried IN ADDITION to the fuel needed to fly to the first point of intended landing (considering wind and forecast weather conditions). They are minimums; they are not total-fuel figures.

1. REGULATORY TEXT (verbatim, 14 CFR § 91.151)

"§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.

(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—

(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or

(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Source verification performed: the text above was read directly from the eCFR current version of § 91.151 (title 14, chapter I, subchapter F, part 91, subpart B), from the GovInfo PDF of the 2026 print edition of 14 CFR volume 2 (CFR-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151), and from the 2025 XML edition of the same section. All three render the airplane figures identically as 30 minutes (day) and 45 minutes (night). No later amendment appears in any fetched source, so the values stated here are current as of the sources retrieved. Paragraph (b) (rotorcraft, 20 minutes) is reproduced only for completeness and does not apply to airplanes.

2. SCOPE AND DEFINITIONS

  • Airplane: § 91.151(a) governs airplanes. Rotorcraft fall under § 91.151(b) (20 minutes, day or night). Do not apply the 20-minute rotorcraft figure to an airplane.
  • Part 91: this is a Part 91 general operating rule. Operations under other parts (e.g., Part 121 or Part 135) are subject to their own fuel-requirement rules; those rules are separate and were not part of the verified source set, so they are not restated here. Do not conflate them with § 91.151.
  • VFR conditions: the rule is triggered by beginning a flight under VFR. It is a pre-departure prohibition — 'no person may begin a flight ... unless' the fuel is aboard at brake release.
  • First point of intended landing: the first airport/landing point planned for the flight (the same concept used in the VFR flight-plan content rule, § 91.153(a)(6), 'the point of first intended landing'). The reserve is computed after arriving at that point, not after the final destination.
  • Normal cruising speed: the reserve is a TIME (30 or 45 minutes) converted to distance/fuel using the airplane's normal cruising speed — not a distance and not a fixed gallon figure. It is a time requirement, so it is aircraft-independent in form and aircraft-specific in fuel quantity.
  • Day / night: use the 14 CFR 1.1 definitions — 'night' means the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time. 'Day' is the balance of the 24-hour period.
  • Day-to-night transition: the rule is written per condition ('during the day' / 'at night'). Conservative and standard practice for a flight that will be airborne at night is to plan the 45-minute night reserve for the flight; the regulation itself does not authorize using 30 minutes for the portion of a flight that will be conducted at night. Flag this as an operating-policy choice, not verbatim regulatory text.

3. HOW TO APPLY — CALCULATION PROCEDURE

Step 1. Compute trip fuel to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather conditions (use forecast winds/temperatures, not still-air figures, where they differ).
Step 2. Compute the reserve fuel quantity as: reserve time (0.5 h day / 0.75 h night) x normal cruising speed fuel flow (in the same units as the airplane's cruise fuel burn). Equivalently, the reserve distance is reserve time x normal cruising true airspeed, then converted to fuel.
Step 3. Required fuel at brake release = Step 1 + Step 2 (plus taxi/takeoff allowance if the operator's procedure accounts for it separately — § 91.151 does not itself prescribe a taxi allowance; including one is conservative and is an operator policy).
Step 4. Compare required fuel to usable fuel aboard at brake release; usable fuel must be at least the Step 3 total. Also confirm the resulting takeoff weight is within limits — § 91.151 sets a fuel floor, not a weight authorization.
Step 5. Record the computation on the flight-planning form (worksheet in section 4).

Worked examples (HYPOTHETICAL numbers for illustration only — they are not regulatory minimums):

  Example A — Day VFR. Normal cruise 120 KTAS, cruise fuel flow 10 gal/h, trip fuel to first intended landing computed with forecast wind = 24 gal.
    Reserve time = 30 min = 0.5 h.
    Reserve fuel = 0.5 h x 10 gal/h = 5.0 gal (equivalently 0.5 h x 120 kt = 60 nm).
    Required at brake release = 24 + 5.0 = 29.0 gal usable.

  Example B — Night VFR, same airplane and same trip.
    Reserve time = 45 min = 0.75 h.
    Reserve fuel = 0.75 h x 10 gal/h = 7.5 gal (equivalently 0.75 h x 120 kt = 90 nm).
    Required at brake release = 24 + 7.5 = 31.5 gal usable.

  Check: 0.5 h x 120 kt = 60 nm and 0.75 h x 120 kt = 90 nm; 0.5 x 10 = 5.0 gal and 0.75 x 10 = 7.5 gal. The night case is exactly 1.5x the day case, consistent with 45 min / 30 min = 1.5.

4. FLIGHT-PLANNING / COMPLIANCE WORKSHEET (fill one per flight)

  Aircraft type/registration: ____________________  Airplane? Y/N (must be Y for this rule)
  Flight is: DAY VFR / NIGHT VFR (if any night portion, plan night)
  Normal cruising speed (KTAS): ______  Cruise fuel flow (gal/h or lb/h): ______
  Trip fuel to FIRST point of intended landing (wind & forecast weather applied): ______
  Required reserve time: 0.5 h (day) / 0.75 h (night)
  Required reserve fuel = reserve time x cruise fuel flow: ______
  Required usable fuel at brake release = trip fuel + reserve fuel: ______
  Usable fuel actually aboard at brake release: ______  (must be >= required)
  Takeoff/landing weight within limits? Y/N
  Pilot-in-command signature/date: ____________________

5. COMMON ERRORS THIS ANSWER GUARDS AGAINST

  • Applying the 20-minute rotorcraft reserve of § 91.151(b) to an airplane. Wrong; airplanes use 30/45.
  • Using the 45-minute IFR figure in § 91.167 as the VFR night reserve. § 91.167 is a different rule for IFR conditions, with a different structure (destination, alternate, then 45 minutes). The VFR night reserve is 45 minutes under § 91.151(a)(2) — coincidentally the same number, but cited to the wrong section if quoted as § 91.167.
  • Treating 30/45 minutes as the TOTAL fuel requirement. It is reserve fuel beyond the fuel to the first point of intended landing.
  • Treating the reserve as a fixed distance or fixed gallon figure. It is a time at normal cruising speed; the fuel quantity scales with the airplane's speed and fuel flow.
  • Computing the reserve at a reduced/holding speed or at a lower-than-normal power setting to shrink the fuel quantity. The rule says normal cruising speed.

6. LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

This answer states the regulatory minimum under § 91.151(a) for airplanes operating under Part 91 in the United States, as verified against the eCFR current version and the 2025 and 2026 printed editions. It does not address: non-U.S. rules; Part 121/135 fuel requirements; IFR fuel requirements (§ 91.167); or operator/pilot personal-minimum policies, which may be more conservative and, when adopted, become the applicable planning figure. § 91.151 sets a floor; a pilot in command may and often should plan above it.
